title: Day and night: why the Sun reaches Guwahati before Mumbai

summary.text: One Sun, one country and one clock, yet the Sun rises over Guwahati about an hour before it rises over Mumbai. You check this with sunrise and sunset times from five cities, and you find a neat pattern hidden in the untidy numbers: the Sun is highest about 4 minutes later for every degree you go west. You measure the spinning Earth on an orange and find that a person in Chennai is carried much faster than a person near the Arctic, though both make one turn a day. Then you follow the spin out to the length of a day on other planets, to a day that is slowly getting longer, and to the animals who live in the dark.
summary.art: A map of India with five glowing clock faces from Guwahati in the east to Mumbai in the west, each showing a time a little later than the one before.

intro.hook: Open a weather app and look at today's sunrise in Guwahati and in Mumbai. Both times are on the same clock, the clock of one country. Yet they are about an hour apart. Did the Sun visit Guwahati first?
intro.text: The Sun did not visit anyone. The Earth is turning, and the Sun's light reaches each place in its turn. In this unit you collect real sunrise and sunset times from five cities and find the pattern in them. You measure how fast the spin carries different places, using an orange. You make a model of why a day is a little longer than one spin. You also find out how the length of a day changes on other planets and over millions of years, and who is awake while we sleep.
intro.art: A phone screen showing two sunrise times, Guwahati and Mumbai, more than an hour apart, held in front of a globe of India.

outcomes: I can explain why the Sun is highest about 4 minutes later for every degree of longitude we go west, and use this to compare two places.
I can work out the time of solar noon from a sunrise time and a sunset time.
I can use an orange model to explain why places near the equator are carried faster than places near the poles, though every place makes one turn a day.
I can explain why Indian Standard Time is a shared agreement, and why clock time and Sun time differ from place to place.
I can explain why the Earth spins once in 23 hours 56 minutes, but the day from one noon to the next is 24 hours.
I can give evidence that the Earth's spin is slowly getting slower, and compare the length of a day on Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Venus.
I can describe two ways that night animals find their way in the dark, and one way that light at night harms them.

terms.meaning: The line that something rotates around. The Earth's axis runs through the North Pole and the South Pole.
terms.example: A skewer pushed through an orange is its axis.

terms.meaning: Turning the opposite way to the hands of a clock. Seen from above the North Pole, the Earth turns anticlockwise, which is from west to east.

terms.meaning: The line between the half of the Earth that is lit by the Sun and the half that is dark.
terms.example: At dawn the line is passing over you.

terms.meaning: How far north or south of the equator a place is, measured in degrees.
terms.art: A globe with horizontal circles drawn at 0, 30 and 60 degrees.

terms.meaning: How far east or west of a line through Greenwich in London a place is, measured in degrees.
terms.example: Chennai is about 80 degrees east. Mumbai is about 73 degrees east.

terms.meaning: The moment when the Sun is at its highest point in the sky at a place. Shadows are shortest then.

explanations.concept: The Earth spins west to east, so the Sun reaches the east first
explanations.definition: The Earth spins once around its axis in about a day, from west to east. So places in the east turn into the sunlight before places in the west.
explanations.description: Seen from above the North Pole, the Earth turns anticlockwise. A place in the east is carried into the sunlit half before a place in the west. That is why the Sun rises in the east, and why Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise before Gujarat does. Half of the Earth is always lit. The day-night line runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. Relative to the ground, it sweeps westward all day and all night. When the dawn part of the line is over Guwahati, Dong in the east is already in daylight, and Mumbai in the west is still in the dark. The line never stops, so at every moment, somewhere on Earth, it is sunrise.
examples: The Sun rises in the east because the ground under us turns towards the east.
Sunrise in Arunachal Pradesh comes more than an hour before sunrise in Gujarat.
At any moment, it is sunrise somewhere on Earth.
explanations.art: The Earth seen from above the North Pole with an anticlockwise arrow, the day-night line drawn, and Dong, Guwahati and Mumbai marked on it.

explanations.concept: The Sun is highest about 4 minutes later for every degree you go west
explanations.definition: The Earth turns 1 degree of longitude in 4 minutes. So solar noon comes about 4 minutes later for each degree of longitude we move west.
explanations.description: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. 24 hours is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 360 is 4. So the Earth turns 1 degree every 4 minutes. Two places that are 1 degree apart in longitude have their solar noon 4 minutes apart. India is about 29 degrees wide, from about 68 degrees east to about 97 degrees east. That is about 116 minutes, nearly two hours. Sunrise gaps are untidy, because sunrise also depends on how far north you are and on the season. In winter, a northern city has a later sunrise and an earlier sunset than a southern one. But the middle of the day, solar noon, depends only on longitude. You can find it by adding the sunrise and sunset times and taking the middle. That is why the noon gaps come out neat.
examples: Chennai is about 4 degrees east of Kochi, so noon comes about 16 minutes earlier in Chennai.
Delhi and Bengaluru are almost on the same line of longitude, so their noons are only about 2 minutes apart, though they are far apart north to south.
Guwahati and Mumbai are about 19 degrees apart, so noon in Mumbai is about 75 minutes later.
explanations.art: A row of five clocks above five cities from east to west, with a bracket between neighbours saying how many minutes later.

explanations.concept: Clock time and Sun time: Indian Standard Time
explanations.definition: Indian Standard Time is the one clock time used all over India. It matches the Sun on the line of longitude 82.5 degrees east, which passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. It is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of the world's reference time, UTC.
explanations.description: Long ago, every town set its clocks by its own Sun. That worked until trains and the telegraph needed timetables that made sense in many towns. In 1906 British India introduced one standard time, Indian Standard Time. Calcutta and Bombay kept their own city clocks for many more years. Today one Indian Standard Time is used for the whole country. On this clock, the Sun is highest at 12 o'clock only on the line 82.5 degrees east. Chennai is about 2 degrees west of that line, so its noon comes about 9 minutes after 12. Guwahati is about 9 degrees east of it, so its noon comes about 37 minutes before 12. Dong, in Arunachal Pradesh, is about 14 degrees east, so its noon comes close to an hour before 12. These noon times are yearly averages. During the year the Sun's noon moves a few minutes either way, but the gaps between cities stay the same. The clock is an agreement among people. The Sun's time belongs to each place. Some tea gardens in Assam have kept their own garden time, one hour ahead of Indian Standard Time, so that work starts at sunrise.
examples: Noon by the Sun in Mumbai is about 12:38, not 12:00.
Noon by the Sun in Guwahati is about 11:23, not 12:00.
Many Assam tea gardens run on garden time, one hour ahead of Indian Standard Time.
explanations.art: A map of India with a vertical line at 82.5 degrees east labelled 12 o'clock noon, and arrows to Guwahati and Mumbai showing the Sun's noon earlier and later.

explanations.concept: How fast you are carried: the same turn, a different circle
explanations.definition: Every place on Earth makes one full turn in a day. A place far from the equator travels round a smaller circle, so it is carried more slowly.
explanations.description: The equator is about 40,075 kilometres around. A person on the equator is carried once round it in 24 hours. 40,075 divided by 24 is about 1,670 kilometres an hour. Move north and the circle that your place makes gets smaller, like the rings on a spinning top. The circle at 60 degrees north, where Oslo and Helsinki lie, is only half as long as the equator. A person there is carried at about 835 kilometres an hour. At the North Pole itself, a person only turns on the spot. Speed depends on latitude, and the nearer you are to the equator, the faster you go. Chennai, at 13 degrees north, is carried at about 1,625 kilometres an hour. Delhi, at 29 degrees north, is carried at about 1,465.
examples: Kochi is carried at about 1,645 kilometres an hour.
Delhi is carried at about 1,465 kilometres an hour.
A person at the North Pole is not carried anywhere. They turn once on the spot.
explanations.art: A globe with three circles drawn at the equator, 30 degrees and 60 degrees north, each labelled with a speed in kilometres an hour.

explanations.concept: Why we feel nothing, and the two small things we can feel
explanations.definition: We feel no spin because it is smooth and steady, and everything around us is carried along too. But the spin does change the Earth's shape and our weight a tiny bit.
explanations.description: In a smooth train, you do not feel the speed. You only feel bumps, starts and stops. The Earth turns smoothly, so there are no bumps. Yet the spin does leave two small marks. First, the spin flings things outward a little, so the Earth is slightly wider across the equator than from pole to pole. The difference is about 43 kilometres. Second, the spin and the bulge together make gravity a tiny bit weaker at the equator. A child who weighs 30 kilograms at the poles weighs about 150 grams less at the equator. That is about the weight of an apple. Scales can show it, but your body cannot feel it.
examples: The Earth is about 12,756 kilometres wide across the equator and about 12,714 kilometres from pole to pole.
A 30 kilogram child weighs about 150 grams less on the equator than at the North Pole.
Spinning a ball of soft clay fast makes it bulge in the middle.
explanations.art: A slightly squashed Earth beside a perfect circle, with a bathroom scale showing a slightly smaller number at the equator than at the pole.

explanations.concept: A day is 24 hours, but the Earth spins once in 23 hours 56 minutes
explanations.definition: One full spin of the Earth takes 23 hours 56 minutes. A day from one noon to the next takes 24 hours. The extra 4 minutes are there because the Earth also moves round the Sun.
explanations.description: While the Earth spins, it also travels round the Sun, once in a year. In one day it moves a little along its path, about 1 degree. After one full spin, the Sun is not yet back overhead, because the Earth has moved. The Earth has to turn about 1 degree more to face the Sun again. At 4 minutes for each degree, that is about 4 minutes more. So one spin takes 23 hours 56 minutes, and the Sun takes 24 hours to come back to the same place in the sky. The faraway stars are so far that the Earth's small move round the Sun does not change where they are. So a star comes back to the same place after exactly one spin. This is why a star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night.
examples: A bright star sets about 4 minutes earlier each night.
After a month, a star sets about 2 hours earlier than at the start.
The same 4 minutes per degree gives both the longitude rule and the star-day rule.
explanations.art: A top-down diagram of the Earth in two positions on its path round the Sun, with an arrow to a faraway star and a small extra angle marked after one spin.

explanations.definition: A planet's day is the time it takes to spin once. It is different on every planet.
explanations.description: Mars spins once in about 24 hours 37 minutes, so a day there is almost like ours. Jupiter is the biggest planet, but it spins once in only about 9 hours 56 minutes. Its edge is carried at more than 40,000 kilometres an hour. Venus spins once in 243 Earth days, which is longer than its year of 225 Earth days. Venus also spins backwards, so the Sun would rise in the west. Why Venus spins this way is not known. Ideas include a giant crash long ago, and the pull of the Sun on its thick air.
examples: On Jupiter, you would have about 2 and a half sunrises in one Earth day.
A day on Mars is about 37 minutes longer than a day on Earth.
On Venus, one spin takes longer than one trip round the Sun.
explanations.art: Four planets in a row, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Venus, each with a clock showing how long one spin takes.

explanations.concept: The Earth's day is slowly getting longer
explanations.definition: The Earth's spin is slowing down. A day gets about 2 thousandths of a second longer every hundred years.
explanations.description: The Moon pulls on the oceans and makes the tides. As the tides move over the sea floor, they rub, like a gentle brake on the spinning Earth. The spin loses energy. The Moon gains it and drifts about 3.8 centimetres further away each year, which scientists measure by bouncing laser light off mirrors that Apollo astronauts left on the Moon. A few thousandths of a second a century sounds like nothing. Over hundreds of millions of years it adds up. In 1963, John Wells counted daily growth lines on fossil corals that lived about 400 million years ago. He found about 400 lines in a year. So the year had about 400 days, and each day was about 22 hours long. Records of ancient eclipses also show the slowing. Big events can change a day too. The 2011 earthquake in Japan moved so much rock that it shortened the day by about 2 millionths of a second.
examples: Corals from 400 million years ago show a year with about 400 days.
The Moon is moving away from the Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year.
The 2011 Japan earthquake shortened the day by about 2 millionths of a second.
explanations.art: A fossil coral with fine daily lines and thicker yearly bands, next to a clock showing a 22 hour day.

explanations.description: Moths and many other insects fly in circles round lamps at night. Scientists agree that the light changes how the insect steers. They do not all agree on how.
examples: Moths circling a tube light on a balcony.
Insects gathering under a streetlight.
Moths flying straight when the Moon is the only light.
explanations.art: A moth spiralling round a lamp at night, with a dotted path.

perspectives.explanation: Insects fly straight by keeping the Moon at the same angle. A lamp is much nearer than the Moon, so as the insect flies past the lamp, the angle keeps changing. The insect turns to fix the angle and ends up spiralling in.

perspectives.who: The back-to-the-light idea (Samuel Fabian and colleagues, 2024)
perspectives.explanation: High-speed cameras showed insects tilting so that their backs face the brightest light. This works well under a bright sky. Near a lamp, it makes them tilt, circle, and sometimes fly upside down.

explanations.concept: Night is full of life, and light can harm it
explanations.definition: Many animals and plants are active at night. Artificial light at night, called light pollution, can confuse them and hide the stars from us.
explanations.description: Night animals solve the problem of the dark in different ways. A barn owl hears the tiny rustle of a mouse with ears set at different heights on her head. A bat shouts and listens to the echoes. A slender loris has huge eyes that gather every bit of light. An Indian rock python feels the warmth of prey with pits on her lips. Fireflies make their own light. Night-blooming flowers such as raat ki rani send out a scent that moths follow. Artificial light disturbs this. Baby olive ridley turtles walk towards the brightest horizon, which should be the sea. Streetlights on a beach can lead them the wrong way. Migrating birds can crash into lit towers. A study in 2016 found that more than 80 percent of people on Earth live under a sky made brighter by artificial light.
examples: Olive ridley turtle hatchlings on Chennai and Odisha beaches can be led away from the sea by lights.
A barn owl can catch a mouse in total darkness by sound alone.
Fireflies flash to find each other, and bright lights make this harder.
explanations.art: A beach at night with baby turtles crawling in two directions, some to the sea and some towards the lights of a road.

agreed.text: The Earth spins once on its axis in about 24 hours, from west to east.
agreed.evidence: A Foucault pendulum, star trails in long photographs, and pictures taken from space all show the spin.

agreed.text: Solar noon comes about 4 minutes later for every degree of longitude we go west.
agreed.evidence: Sunrise and sunset tables for cities around the world, and world time zones, all follow this rule. 360 degrees in 24 hours is 4 minutes a degree.

agreed.text: Every place makes one turn a day, so places far from the equator are carried more slowly than places near it.
agreed.evidence: The Earth's size has been measured by surveyors and satellites. A smaller circle covered in the same time means a slower speed.

agreed.text: The Earth's spin is slowing by about 2 thousandths of a second each century, mainly because of the tides raised by the Moon.
agreed.evidence: Records of eclipses made over 2,700 years, growth lines in fossil corals and shells, and atomic clocks all agree.

agreed.text: Artificial light at night changes the behaviour of many animals, including turtles, birds and insects.
agreed.evidence: Studies on beaches, on migration routes and under streetlights have measured the changes.

challenging.claim: The Sun is highest at 12 o'clock everywhere in India.
challenging.who: Many people, because every clock in the country says 12.
challenging.for: All of India uses one clock time, so it feels like the same moment everywhere.
challenging.against: Noon by the Sun is about 11:23 in Guwahati and about 12:38 in Mumbai. The clock is an agreement. The Sun's time belongs to each place.

challenging.claim: India should have two time zones.
challenging.who: Some people in the north-east of India, and some scientists.
challenging.for: In the east, the Sun rises very early and sets early. In winter it is dark soon after 4 in the afternoon, so people lose daylight in the evening, and children may walk home from school in the dark.
challenging.against: Two clocks inside one country could confuse trains, flights, banks and phone systems. Many people prefer the simplicity of one time.

challenging.claim: Everything on Earth moves at the same speed as the Earth spins.
challenging.for: Everything makes one turn in the same 24 hours.
challenging.against: The circle you travel is longer near the equator and shorter near the poles, so the speed is different. A person on the equator is carried about twice as fast as a person at 60 degrees north.

challenging.claim: A day has always been 24 hours long.
challenging.who: Almost everyone, because clocks have always said 24.
challenging.for: Within a human life, the length of the day looks fixed.
challenging.against: Fossil corals, eclipse records and the Moon's slow drift show that days were shorter long ago. About 400 million years ago a day was about 22 hours.

challenging.claim: Moths fly round lamps because they are confused about the Moon.
challenging.who: A popular explanation for many years.
challenging.for: It is neat, and some experiments seem to fit it.
challenging.against: High-speed cameras in 2024 suggested that the light makes insects tilt their backs towards it, which makes them circle. Scientists are still testing this.

big_questions.q: It is always sunrise somewhere on Earth. So where does a day begin?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dawn line moving round the Earth, and where people agreed to start counting.

big_questions.q: In Guwahati the Sun is highest at 11:23 and in Mumbai at 12:38, and all the clocks say 12. Is noon a fact about the Sun, or an agreement between people?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would stay the same if everyone changed their clocks.

big_questions.q: A plane flying west near the Arctic Circle at about 670 kilometres an hour can keep up with the Sun's spin. What would you see out of the window, and what does this say about how fast the Earth turns there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the small circle at the Arctic and your orange.

big_questions.q: In the north-east in winter, the Sun sets before 5 in the afternoon, so children may walk home in the dark, though the Sun was up before most of them woke. Should a country's clock follow the Sun, or follow what is easy to share?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gains and who loses with each choice.

big_questions.q: Streetlights make cities safer for people, and they confuse turtles, birds and insects. Who should the night belong to?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is asked, and who is not.

big_questions.q: The Earth's spin gives us day and night. What gave the Earth its spin in the first place, and why has it not stopped?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cloud the Sun and planets formed from, and what is around the Earth to slow it.

story.title: The Morning That Was on Its Way
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Port Blair is about 12 degrees of longitude east of Chennai. The line of dawn sweeps west at about 4 minutes for each degree, so it reaches Chennai about fifty minutes after Port Blair. Chennai faces the Bay of Bengal on its east side, so the Sun there rises over the sea. Kavya, Patti and Rajam are imagined.
text: When Patti came to live with us in Chennai, she brought two suitcases, a brass lamp and a habit of waking before five o'clock.

For fifty years, Patti had lived in Port Blair, on the Andaman Islands. There the sky turns gold early, long before most of India has woken. Her little sister, Rajam, still lives there, in a house above the harbour.
On her first morning in our flat, Patti sat at the east window with her tea. It was grey and dark outside. The sea was only a darker darkness beyond the rooftops. She waited, and nothing happened.
'This Sun is lazy,' she said. 'At home it would be up by now.'
She said it the next morning too, and the morning after. Slowly her tea went cold in her hands. I was nine, and I did not know what to say.
Every morning, Patti rang Rajam. And every day Rajam sent a photograph from her window: the sea, the sky, a ribbon of orange. Patti looked at it for a long time.
'My sister's morning is already over,' she said once. 'Here it is only starting. I am always late in this city.'

That week at school, our teacher, Ms Hema, gave us a puzzle. She turned the classroom globe slowly. 'The Earth turns all the way round, three hundred and sixty degrees, in twenty-four hours,' she said. 'How many minutes is that for one degree?'
We worked it out on our slates. Twenty-four hours is one thousand four hundred and forty minutes. Divided by three hundred and sixty, it is four. The Earth turns one degree every four minutes.

That night, at home, I took the globe from my shelf. I put one thread on Port Blair and one on Chennai. I counted the degrees of longitude between them. There were about twelve. Twelve times four is forty-eight.
I looked at the number for a long time. Forty-eight minutes. Not lazy. Not late. Just on its way.
The next morning I woke Patti at ten to five. 'Patti, come to the window. Please.'
She came, grumbling, in her nightdress. Her phone buzzed on the sill. It was Rajam's photograph. The sky over the harbour was bright gold.

'Look at the photograph,' I said. 'That is the dawn at Rajam's window. It is moving west, over the sea, at the speed of the turning Earth. It is coming here. In about forty-eight minutes, it will be at our window.'
Patti looked at me. She looked at the phone. Then she looked out at the grey. 'The same dawn?'
'The same line of dawn,' I said. 'It never stops. It is leaving her window now, and it is coming to ours.'

We sat together and waited. Patti held her cold tea. The crows began first. Then a thin pale line appeared on the sea, far out. It grew. It turned pink and then orange, and then a bright gold light came over the water and across the rooftops and into our window. It touched Patti's hands.
'There,' said Patti, very quietly. 'Rajam's morning has come.'
She did not say anything for a while. Then she laughed. 'So I am not late. I am only downstream.'
A week later, it rained. The sky over Chennai was thick with cloud. Patti stood at the window and her face fell. 'It has not come. The cloud has stopped it.'
I thought about this. 'The cloud hides it,' I said. 'It cannot stop it. The Earth does not wait for the sky to be clear. The dawn is already here, behind the cloud. We just cannot see it.'
Patti rang Rajam. 'Is it clear there?' she asked. 'It was? Good. Then my morning is here, in the rain. I can feel it.'
Patti pointed at the globe, which I had brought to the window. 'And after us?'
I turned it with my finger. 'After us, it goes on to Kochi. Then Mumbai, then over the Arabian Sea. Then it reaches Africa, and it keeps going all the way round.'
'So every morning I have is passed along to someone else,' said Patti.
'Yes,' I said. 'And every morning someone passes one to us.'
From then on, she woke at five every day, and we sat at the window and waited for Rajam's morning. Sometimes we saw it. Sometimes the cloud hid it. But Patti never said that the Sun was lazy again.
story.epiphany: A sunrise is not an event that happens to a whole country at once. It is a line of dawn that crosses the Earth and never stops. It reaches each place about 4 minutes later for every degree of longitude to the west. So Rajam's sunrise in Port Blair reached Chennai about fifty minutes later.
ask: The line of dawn reaches a city at 5:30 by the clock. About when does it reach a city 10 degrees of longitude to the west?
If thick cloud hides the sunrise, has the line of dawn stopped? Why or why not?
Where on Earth is the line of dawn right now, and which way is it moving?

roots.context: We have followed the Sun's light round the spinning Earth, from Guwahati to Mumbai. Now we ask what this tells us about morning, about time, and about our own place in it.

deep_truth.truth: Sunrise is not an event that happens to a whole country at once. It is a line that crosses the Earth and never stops. The dawn that reached Guwahati arrived in Mumbai about an hour later. So morning belongs to a place, and no one moment is morning for everyone.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the Sun rises at 6' as if morning were one thing that happens to everyone together. One clock for a whole country hides the fact that each place has its own morning, and that the Sun's time and the clock's time are different things.
deep_truth.evidence: In the noon table, the Sun was highest about 4 minutes later for every degree west. Five cities under one Sun and one clock had five different noons. And because the Earth keeps turning, a dawn is always crossing somewhere.

three.who_am_i: You are not waiting for the morning to come to you. You are being carried through it, at about 1,500 kilometres an hour, on a turning Earth.
three.what_is_life: Birds, flowers and people wake as the dawn reaches them. Many birds start singing as the light arrives, so a wave of birdsong travels with the line of dawn round the world.
three.what_is_this_world: There is one Sun and one turning Earth. So a line of dawn and a line of dusk are always crossing the planet, and somewhere it is always morning.

roots.thread: From one Sun comes light, and from one turning Earth comes a dawn that passes from place to place. No place owns the morning. Each place receives it a few minutes after its eastern neighbour, and passes it on to the west. The many mornings are one morning, handed on. This is the one becoming the many in time. A single dawn line, circling the world, becomes a different time of day for every place it crosses.

teachings.teaching: This hymn to Night and Dawn describes them as two sisters who follow each other across the sky. They look different, but they work together and are never apart for long.
teachings.link: Night and dawn are made by one turning Earth. The dawn line is the border where one sister meets the other.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus wrote that the Sun is new every day.
teachings.link: The sunrise that reaches you today is a new meeting between you and the light. Yet it is one dawn line that has been circling the Earth for billions of years.

science.text: The Earth turns 1 degree in 4 minutes, so the Sun reaches the places along a line of latitude in turn. Time zones and Indian Standard Time are human agreements laid over this.
Einstein showed in 1905 that for places far apart, 'at the same time' depends on how the observers are moving. On Earth the effect is far too small to notice.

other_view.view: For everyday life, one shared time works perfectly well. Atomic clocks keep a single world time called UTC, and every place can tell its Sun time from it. They would say the line of dawn is only geometry, and that there is nothing deeper to find in it.

practice.title: Facing the dawn line
practice.say: Stand or sit at a window that faces east, early in the morning. If it is dark, close your eyes. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. Feel the ground under you being carried towards the east. Say quietly in your mind: the light is coming to me from the east. Somewhere to my east, someone is seeing it now. Breathe three more times and open your eyes.
practice.kid: Face east at a window. Breathe slowly three times. Feel the Earth carrying you towards the light. Think: someone to the east is seeing it now.

ask: If it is always sunrise somewhere, is there a first morning of the day?
Is 6 o'clock a fact about the Sun, or an agreement between people? How would you tell?
Which clock should a country keep: the one that matches the Sun at its middle, or one for each place?

games.title: Chase the Dawn: how many minutes later is noon?
games.context: This is a card game about the rule you found in the Five Noons test. Each card names two places. You guess how many minutes later the Sun is highest in the western place.

setup.art: Eighteen cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with four coloured tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. Then read the back.

printables.title: 18 two-sided cards: two places and their longitudes on the front, the answer on the back

items.f: Port Blair (92.7 degrees east) and Chennai (80.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Chennai?
items.b: About 50 minutes. 92.7 minus 80.3 is 12.4 degrees. 12.4 times 4 is about 50. Token: 30 to 60 minutes.

items.f: Kolkata (88.4 degrees east) and Kochi (76.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Kochi?
items.b: About 48 minutes. 88.4 minus 76.3 is 12.1 degrees. 12.1 times 4 is about 48. Token: 30 to 60 minutes.

items.f: Guwahati (91.7 degrees east) and Mumbai (72.9 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Mumbai?
items.b: About 75 minutes. 91.7 minus 72.9 is 18.8 degrees. 18.8 times 4 is about 75. Token: more than 60 minutes.

items.f: Kohima (94.1 degrees east) and Dwarka (69.0 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Dwarka?
items.b: About 100 minutes, which is 1 hour 40 minutes. 94.1 minus 69.0 is 25.1 degrees. 25.1 times 4 is about 100. Token: more than 60 minutes.

items.f: Delhi (77.2 degrees east) and Bengaluru (77.6 degrees east). Which is first, and by how many minutes?
items.b: Bengaluru is first, by about 2 minutes. They are on almost the same line of longitude, so how far north or south they are does not matter. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Hyderabad (78.5 degrees east) and Chennai (80.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Hyderabad?
items.b: About 7 minutes. 80.3 minus 78.5 is 1.8 degrees. 1.8 times 4 is about 7. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Kolkata (88.4 degrees east) and Visakhapatnam (83.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Visakhapatnam?
items.b: About 20 minutes. 88.4 minus 83.3 is 5.1 degrees. 5.1 times 4 is about 20. Token: 10 to 30 minutes.

items.f: Dong in Arunachal Pradesh (97.0 degrees east) and Guwahati (91.7 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Guwahati?
items.b: About 21 minutes. 97.0 minus 91.7 is 5.3 degrees. 5.3 times 4 is about 21. Token: 10 to 30 minutes.

items.f: Chennai (80.3 degrees east) and Madurai (78.1 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Madurai?
items.b: About 9 minutes. 80.3 minus 78.1 is 2.2 degrees. 2.2 times 4 is about 9. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Kochi (76.3 degrees east) and Mangaluru (74.9 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Mangaluru?
items.b: About 6 minutes. 76.3 minus 74.9 is 1.4 degrees. 1.4 times 4 is about 6. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Delhi (77.2 degrees east) and Jaipur (75.8 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Jaipur?
items.b: About 6 minutes. 77.2 minus 75.8 is 1.4 degrees. 1.4 times 4 is about 6. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Guwahati (91.7 degrees east) and Shillong (91.9 degrees east). Is the Sun highest at about the same time in both?
items.b: Yes, within 1 minute. They are only 0.2 degrees apart, and 0.2 times 4 is under 1 minute. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: India is about 29 degrees wide from east to west. About how many minutes between the Sun's highest in the far east and in the far west?
items.b: About 116 minutes, nearly 2 hours. 29 times 4 is 116. Token: more than 60 minutes.

items.f: Thiruvananthapuram (76.9 degrees east) and Kochi (76.3 degrees east). Which is first, and by how many minutes?
items.b: Thiruvananthapuram is first, by about 2 minutes. 76.9 minus 76.3 is 0.6 degrees. 0.6 times 4 is about 2. Token: under 10 minutes.

items.f: Kolkata (88.4 degrees east) and Chennai (80.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Chennai?
items.b: About 32 minutes. 88.4 minus 80.3 is 8.1 degrees. 8.1 times 4 is about 32. Token: 30 to 60 minutes.

items.f: Guwahati (91.7 degrees east) and Chennai (80.3 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Chennai?
items.b: About 46 minutes. 91.7 minus 80.3 is 11.4 degrees. 11.4 times 4 is about 46. Token: 30 to 60 minutes.

items.f: Hyderabad (78.5 degrees east) and Mumbai (72.9 degrees east). How many minutes later is the Sun highest in Mumbai?
items.b: About 22 minutes. 78.5 minus 72.9 is 5.6 degrees. 5.6 times 4 is about 22. Token: 10 to 30 minutes.

items.f: Indian Standard Time is set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. Dong is at 97.0 degrees east. About how many minutes before 12 o'clock is the Sun highest in Dong?
items.b: About 58 minutes before. 97.0 minus 82.5 is 14.5 degrees. 14.5 times 4 is 58. Token: 30 to 60 minutes.

printables.title: 4 tokens for each player: Under 10 minutes, 10 to 30 minutes, 30 to 60 minutes, More than 60 minutes

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player has four tokens. Each player puts one token face down. It is a guess of how many minutes later the Sun is highest in the western place.
When everyone has chosen, turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back, which names the right token.
A player whose token is right scores one point. A player who also says the exact number of minutes, within 5 minutes, scores one more point.
With two players, the parent and the child swap the reader's job after every card. The reader never guesses on their own card.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left.
The game ends when all 18 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 18 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player a set of four tokens.
flow.say: These cards have two places on them. We guess how many minutes later the Sun is highest in the western place. Each player gets four tokens.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take four tokens each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Chase the Dawn. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first five cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone puts a token face down. Turn them over together. Then the reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do you multiply by to turn degrees of longitude into minutes?

flow.context: In this step, you play the first five cards and learn how the scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next seven cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Remember that the gap in degrees times 4 is the gap in minutes.
flow.kid: Play on. Gap in degrees, times four, gives the minutes.

ask.q: Which card surprised you, and why?
good: Delhi and Bengaluru are so close.

flow.parent: The Delhi and Bengaluru card is the surprise for most families. They are far apart north to south, but the Sun reaches them almost together, because only east and west matter.
flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Is the western place always later? What about when two places are the same longitude?
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card was hardest to guess, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was hardest? Why was it hard?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Could two places far apart north to south have the same noon?
flow.context: This is the last step of Chase the Dawn. You look back at the game.

games.title: Night Shift: how does this animal find the way in the dark?
games.context: This is a guessing game about animals that are awake at night. Each card names an animal and a problem. You guess which of six senses or tools solves it.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with six tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a night animal and the problem she must solve on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: A barn owl hunts mice in a dark field. How does she find one?
items.b: Ears. Her ears sit at different heights on her head, so she can tell where a tiny rustle is coming from.

items.f: A small bat catches insects in the dark above a city street. How does she find them?
items.b: Ears. She shouts in a very high voice and listens to the echoes that come back.

items.f: A male cricket sings in the grass. How does a female cricket find him?
items.b: Ears. A cricket has her ears on her front legs, and she listens for the song.

items.f: After the first rains, a female frog looks for a calling male in a pond at night. How does she find him?
items.b: Ears. She listens for the call of her own kind and walks towards it.

items.f: A hawk moth looks for a night-blooming jasmine, the raat ki rani, in a dark garden. How does she find it?
items.b: Nose. The flower gives out a strong scent at night, and she follows it with her antennae.

items.f: A street dog finds a dropped piece of roti in the dark. How?
items.b: Nose. A dog's sense of smell is far stronger than ours.

items.f: An Indian cobra flicks out her tongue as she moves through the dark. What is she doing?
items.b: Nose. She collects tiny scent particles on her tongue and tastes them at the roof of her mouth.

items.f: A slender loris climbs through trees at night in the forests of South India. How does she see?
items.b: Eyes. Her eyes are huge and gather every scrap of light.

items.f: A house gecko waits beside a tube light on a wall. How does she spot a moth?
items.b: Eyes. Her eyes work in dim light, and some geckos can even see colours at night.

items.f: A leopard walks through a forest at night. How does she see her way?
items.b: Eyes. A mirror-like layer at the back of her eyes bounces light back, so she uses the light twice.

items.f: A baby olive ridley turtle hatches on a beach at night. How does she find the sea?
items.b: Eyes. She crawls towards the brightest, lowest horizon, which is normally the open sea. Streetlights can fool her.

items.f: An Indian rock python lies in wait at night. How does she sense a warm rat?
items.b: Heat. She has pits on her lips that feel the warmth of living bodies.

items.f: A pit viper in the Western Ghats strikes in the dark. How does she aim?
items.b: Heat. She has two pits on her face that sense the warmth of her prey.

items.f: A scorpion waits on sandy ground at night. How does she know an insect is near?
items.b: Touch. She feels tiny shaking in the sand through her legs.

items.f: A cat squeezes through a dark gap between two cupboards. How does she know it is wide enough?
items.b: Touch. Her whiskers brush the sides and tell her how wide the gap is.

items.f: An orb spider sits on the edge of her web at night. How does she know an insect has landed?
items.b: Touch. She feels the web shake through her legs.

items.f: A mouse runs along a wall in a dark kitchen. How does he know where the wall is?
items.b: Touch. His whiskers brush the wall as he runs.

items.f: A firefly flashes in a dark field. How does she make herself seen by a mate?
items.b: Light. She makes her own cold light inside her body.

items.f: A small sea creature called Noctiluca glows blue when waves disturb it on some Indian beaches. What is she using?
items.b: Light. She makes her own light, which is why the waves seem to sparkle.

items.f: An anglerfish lives in the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches. How does she attract fish?
items.b: Light. She has a glowing lure on her head, lit by glowing bacteria that live in the lure.
