experiments.title: Five Noons: is the Sun highest at the same moment in every city?
experiments.question: The clocks in Guwahati, Kolkata, Chennai, Kochi and Mumbai all show the same time. Is the Sun at its highest in all five cities at the same clock time?
experiments.predict: Before you look at any data, guess. Will the Sun be at its highest at the same clock time in all five cities? If not, which city comes first, which comes last, and how far apart are they? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same date for all five cities and the same source for the times, such as one weather app. Read each time to the minute. Work out noon in the same way for every city. Only the city changes, so any difference in noon comes from where the city is.

materials.item: a phone, tablet or computer with a weather app or the website timeanddate.com, or today's newspaper with its weather box
paper, a pencil and the results table (draw it on paper or print it from the app)
the list of longitudes: Guwahati 91.7, Kolkata 88.4, Chennai 80.3, Kochi 76.3 and Mumbai 72.9 degrees east
a calculator, if you want one

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all five cities. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each city. The bar shows how many minutes later than Guwahati the Sun is highest there.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you collect real sunrise and sunset times for five cities, work out when the Sun is highest in each, and look for a pattern.

setup.art: A phone screen showing sunrise and sunset times for Chennai, held beside a notebook with a table drawn in it.
setup.caption: 1. Look up sunrise and sunset for each of the five cities, on the same day.

setup.art: A notebook page showing one row of the table: sunrise 6:10, sunset 17:50, a line between them with the middle marked as noon.
setup.caption: 2. Find the middle of the day for each city. This is noon by the Sun.

setup.art: A map of India with five dots from Guwahati to Mumbai, each with its longitude and a noon time written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the noons with the longitudes and look for the pattern.

flow.do: Show your child the five cities on a map. Tell them the clocks in all five show the same time. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: All five cities use the same clock. Will the Sun be at its highest at the same time in all of them? If not, which city is first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five cities, one clock. Is the Sun highest at the same time in all? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the noons will be the same, or different?
good: The Sun gets to the east first.
Guwahati is nearer the Sun's rising place.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say the noons are the same, because the clock is the same. That is a good guess to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Five Noons test. You guess before you look at any data.

flow.do: Look up today's sunrise and sunset in each of the five cities. Write each time to the minute. Use the 24-hour clock for sunset, so 5:58 in the evening is 17:58.
flow.say: Look up the sunrise and the sunset for each city. Use the same day and the same app for all five. Write the times to the minute.
flow.kid: Find sunrise and sunset for each city. Write them in the table.
flow.parent: No phone? Use the weather box in a newspaper, or ring a relative in another city and ask when the Sun rose and set. If a city is missing, use any city whose longitude you can look up. Apps can differ from each other by a minute or two. That is fine. Working together: with 2 to 4 children, give each child one or two cities to look up and write on the shared table, then check each other's times. One child on their own does all five cities.

check.q: Why do we use the same date and the same app for all five cities?
options: So that only the city changes
So that the numbers look neat
Because the app only works once a day
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the dates or the apps were different, we would not know whether a difference came from the city or from the date.

flow.context: In this step, you collect real sunrise and sunset times for the five cities.

flow.do: Work out noon for the first city. Count the time from sunrise to sunset. Halve it. Add the half to the sunrise. The answer is when the Sun is highest.
flow.say: Here is a way to find the middle of the day. Count how long it is from sunrise to sunset. Cut that time in half. Add the half to the sunrise time.
flow.kid: Find the middle of the day. Halve the daytime, then add it to sunrise.
flow.parent: Worked example with made-up numbers: sunrise 6:10 and sunset 17:50. From 6:10 to 17:50 is 11 hours 40 minutes. Half of that is 5 hours 50 minutes. 6:10 plus 5:50 is 12:00. So noon is at 12:00. The Sun is highest in the middle of the daytime, so the middle is noon.

check.q: Sunrise is at 6:00 and sunset is at 18:30. When is noon by the Sun?
check.why: From 6:00 to 18:30 is 12 hours 30 minutes. Half is 6 hours 15 minutes. 6:00 plus 6:15 is 12:15.

flow.context: In this step, you learn how to work out noon from sunrise and sunset, using one city.

flow.do: Work out noon for the other four cities. Then, for each city, write how many minutes later than Guwahati its noon is.
flow.say: Do the same for the other four cities. Then count how many minutes later each noon is than the noon in Guwahati.
flow.kid: Find noon for every city. Count the minutes after Guwahati.
flow.parent: Expect Guwahati to be first and Mumbai last. Your gaps should be roughly 13 minutes to Kolkata, 46 to Chennai, 62 to Kochi and 75 to Mumbai, though your numbers may be a minute or two different. A quick check: timeanddate.com also shows the solar noon of each city. If your noon is more than 3 minutes away from that, look at your sum again.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the table, using the same method for every city.

flow.do: Divide each gap in minutes by the gap in degrees of longitude from Guwahati. For Mumbai, that is the gap in minutes divided by 19 degrees, which is about 91.7 minus 72.9. What number do you keep getting?
flow.say: Look at the longitudes. Divide each gap in minutes by the gap in degrees from Guwahati. What number do you keep getting?
flow.kid: Divide minutes by degrees for each city. What number do you get?

ask.q: What do you notice about the minutes for each degree?
good: The further west, the later the noon.

check.q: Noon in Guwahati is at 11:30. Mumbai is 19 degrees of longitude to the west. About when is noon in Mumbai?
options: About 11:30
About 12:00
About 12:45
check.why: 19 degrees times 4 minutes is 76 minutes. 11:30 plus 76 minutes is about 12:46. A wrong answer of 11:30 would mean the noon is the same everywhere, which the data show is not true.

flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern between noon and longitude.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw in the data and why it happened. Then look at the sunrise gaps.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you find? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you found, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that noon came later for every city to the west, by about 4 minutes for each degree. The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, which is 4 minutes for each degree. The sunrise gaps are untidy because sunrise also depends on how far north a city is and on the season. For example, in winter Guwahati is further north than Chennai, so its sunrise comes later than the noon pattern alone would give. The seasons are in the Seasons unit. Noon depends on longitude alone, so it is neat.
flow.think: The sunrise times were not as neat as the noon times. Why might that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Five Noons test. You explain your result.

experiments.title: The Orange Earth: does every place on Earth move at the same speed?
experiments.question: Every place on Earth goes round once in 24 hours. Does a place on the equator move at the same speed as a place far to the north?
experiments.predict: Before you measure, guess. Will a person far to the north be carried faster than, slower than or at the same speed as a person on the equator? And how much slower, if you think so? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three circles are drawn on the same orange and measured with the same thread and ruler. Every spot on the orange turns once in the same time, so a longer circle means a faster spot. Only the latitude of the circle changes.

materials.item: one large orange, round and not too soft, with its stem dimple still showing
a reel of thin sewing thread, about 1 metre (not stretchy wool, which stretches and spoils the lengths)
1 rubber band that fits around the orange
a marker pen (a ballpoint often skips on the oily peel), a ruler and scissors
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up should help with the scissors if your child is young. Draw on the peel only, and do not eat the orange afterwards. Wash your hands after using the pen, and after handling the orange if your child has sensitive skin or a citrus allergy.
experiments.record: Fill in the table with the three lengths. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each circle.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you draw circles on an orange to stand in for the Earth, and measure them to find out which places are carried fastest as the Earth spins.

setup.art: A hand holding an orange, with a marker dot on the stem dimple labelled North Pole and a rubber band around the fattest part.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the poles. Put a rubber band round the middle and draw the equator.

setup.art: A thread laid along the orange skin from the equator line up to the North Pole dot, with a ruler beside it measuring its length.
setup.caption: 2. Measure from the equator to the pole. Mark one third and two thirds of the way up.

setup.art: The orange with three drawn circles, the equator, a middle circle and a small circle near the top.
setup.caption: 3. Join the dots you marked with a pen line all the way round, to draw each circle.

setup.art: A thread wrapped around the equator of the orange, then stretched straight next to a ruler.
setup.caption: 4. Wrap a thread round each circle, cut it, and measure it.

flow.do: Show your child the orange and say it stands in for the Earth. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Every place on Earth goes round once in 24 hours. A person on the equator and a person far to the north go round once each day. Do they move at the same speed? Why?
flow.kid: Everyone on Earth goes round once a day. Is everyone moving at the same speed? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think they move at the same speed, or at different speeds?
good: The circle near the equator is bigger.
The north is closer to the middle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say everybody moves at the same speed because everybody takes a day. That is a good guess to test. One child with a parent: the child does the drawing and measuring, and the parent holds the orange. With 2 to 4 children, give each pair or child their own orange (they are cheap) and share the three lengths on one chart, which also shows how much the oranges differ. Or split the roles: one holds, one draws, one threads and measures.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Orange Earth test. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: The dimple where the stem was is the North Pole. Mark a dot on the opposite end for the South Pole. Slip a rubber band round the fattest part and move it until it is the same distance from both poles. Draw a line along it.
flow.say: The small dimple is the North Pole. Mark the other end as the South Pole. Put a rubber band round the middle. Draw a line along it. This line is the equator.
flow.kid: Mark the two poles. Draw the equator with a rubber band.
flow.parent: To check the band is in the middle, lay a thread from the North Pole dot to the band, and compare it with a thread from the South Pole dot to the band. They should be the same length. An orange is never perfectly round, so be happy with close.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the poles and draw the equator on the orange.

flow.do: Lay a thread along the skin from the equator line up to the North Pole dot, and cut it. Measure it with the ruler. Work out one third and two thirds of its length. Mark both points on four sides of the orange, with a dot each.
flow.say: Lay a thread from the equator up to the North Pole. Cut it and measure it. Mark one third and two thirds of the way up, on four sides.
flow.kid: Measure from the equator to the pole. Mark one third and two thirds.
flow.parent: The way from the equator to the pole is one quarter of the way round the Earth, which is 90 degrees. One third of it is 30 degrees of latitude. Two thirds of it is 60 degrees. For a 6 centimetre thread, mark 2 and 4 centimetres from the equator. Delhi is close to the 30 degree circle. Oslo and Helsinki are close to the 60 degree circle.

check.q: The thread from the equator to the pole is 6 centimetres long. Where is the mark for two thirds of the way?
options: 4 centimetres from the equator
3 centimetres from the equator
5 centimetres from the equator
check.why: Two thirds of 6 is 4, because 6 divided by 3 is 2 and 2 times 2 is 4.

flow.context: In this step, you mark two more circles on the orange, one third and two thirds of the way from the equator to the pole.

flow.do: Mark dots at one third of the way up, on eight sides, all the same height above the equator. Join the dots with a pen line. Do the same at two thirds. You now have three circles.
flow.say: Make a ring of eight dots at the same height above the equator, then join them with a line round the orange. Do the same for the other set of marks. Now you have three circles.
flow.kid: Join the dots into a circle. Do this for both new circles.
flow.parent: A rubber band slides towards the pole on a small circle, so do not use it here. Instead measure the same distance up from the equator line at eight places and join the dots by eye, with a thread laid along them as a guide. A wavy line is fine. If it wanders, measure a few more dots.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the 30 degree circle and the 60 degree circle by joining dots.

flow.do: Wrap a thread round the equator, snip it where it meets itself, and lay it straight along the ruler. Write its length. Do the same for the other two circles.
flow.say: Wrap a thread once round the equator. Snip it, straighten it and measure it. Do the same for the other circles.
flow.kid: Wrap, snip and measure the thread for each circle. Write the lengths.
flow.parent: Typical numbers: an orange about 24 to 26 centimetres round the equator, about 21 to 23 round the 30 degree circle, and about 12 to 13 round the 60 degree circle. Your numbers will not be exact: anything from 40 to 60 out of 100 for the 60 degree circle is a fair result. If the thread stretches or slips off the circle, measure again.

check.q: Each spot on the orange turns once in the same time. Which spot is carried fastest?
options: The one on the longest circle
The one on the shortest circle
They are all carried at the same speed
check.why: A spot on a longer circle has further to go in the same time, so it must move faster. A wrong answer of the same speed would mean that circle size does not matter, which the thread shows is not true.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the length of the three circles.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they measured and why. Then ask how long the 60 degree circle is compared with the equator.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you find? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you found, and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the 60 degree circle is about half as long as the equator, so a spot on it goes half as fast. The 30 degree circle is about 87 out of 100, so those places go about 87 percent as fast. The equator of the real Earth is about 40,075 kilometres. 40,075 divided by 24 is about 1,670 kilometres an hour. Half of that is about 835. A person at the North Pole only turns once on the spot. Real fruit is not a perfect sphere, so do not worry if your answer is a little off half.
flow.think: If the equator is carried at 1,670 kilometres an hour, how fast is a person at the 60 degree circle?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Orange Earth test. You explain your result.

activities.title: The Extra Turn: why a day is a little longer than one spin

materials.item: a torch or table lamp on a low table or stool in the middle of a room
a sticky note with a star drawn on it, stuck to the far wall at your child's eye height (use tape if it does not stick)
8 sheets of paper or old newspaper pages, each with an arrow drawn on it, laid in a circle around the lamp about 1 metre away from it
a clear floor, about 3 metres across

schedule.what: Set up the lamp and the star. Turn on the spot. Then turn while walking round the lamp. Notice the extra turn.

activities.record: Draw the circle, the lamp and the star. Draw an arrow showing which way you turned, and mark the extra bit you had to turn.
activities.context: In this activity, you use your own body to find out why the Earth must turn a little more than once to bring the Sun back to the same place in the sky.

setup.art: A torch on a low table in the middle of a room, eight coins in a circle around it, and a sticky note with a star on the far wall behind the torch.
setup.caption: 1. Put the lamp in the middle. Make a circle of eight marks. Stick a star on the far wall.

setup.art: A child standing on the first mark, facing the lamp, with the star on the wall straight behind the lamp.
setup.caption: 2. Stand on the first mark. The lamp and the star are in the same direction.

setup.art: A child turning once on the spot, then turning once while stepping to the next mark, ending up facing the star but not the lamp.
setup.caption: 3. Turn once while stepping to the next mark. You face the star, but not the lamp.

flow.do: Put the torch on a low table in the middle of the room. Lay out eight marks in a circle around it, with every arrow on every mark pointing the same way, at the star. Stick the star on the far wall, straight behind the lamp from the first mark.
flow.say: The lamp is the Sun. The star on the wall is a faraway star. You are the Earth. Stand on the first mark and face the lamp. The star is right behind it.
flow.kid: The lamp is the Sun. The star is on the wall. Stand on mark one and face the lamp.
flow.parent: The star on the wall stands for a star so far away that it always lies in the same direction. The lamp is close. That is why the lamp changes direction as you move round it, but the star does not. Every arrow points the same way. That is what far away means: from every mark the star lies in the same direction, while the lamp is close and changes direction. The star wall should be at least 4 metres from the lamp if you can manage, but the arrows make a smaller room work too. Facing the star means lining your feet up with the arrow. With 2 to 4 children, one turns while the others watch and say what they see, then swap. Turn and walk anticlockwise (against the way clock hands go), as seen from above.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Extra Turn. You set up the Sun, the star and the Earth.

flow.do: Ask your child to turn once, slowly, on the spot, anticlockwise (to their left), until they face the star again. Ask what they are facing.
flow.say: Turn once slowly to your left, without moving your feet, until you face the star again. What do you face now?
flow.kid: Turn once to your left on the spot. What do you face now?

ask.q: After one full turn on the spot, are you facing the star, the lamp, or both?
good: Both. They are in the same direction.
The star, and the lamp behind it.

flow.parent: If the Earth did not move round the Sun, one spin would bring the Sun back exactly. The star and the lamp are in line, so your child faces both.
flow.context: In this step, you turn once on the spot, with the Earth still in one place.

flow.do: Go back to the first mark. Ask your child to turn once anticlockwise, and walk anticlockwise round the lamp to the next mark as they turn. Stop with your feet along the arrow, facing the star.
flow.say: Now the Earth moves round the Sun too. Turn once anticlockwise as you walk anticlockwise round the lamp to the next mark. Stop with your feet along the arrow, facing the star. Are you facing the lamp?
flow.kid: Turn once anticlockwise as you walk to the next mark. Stop. Are you facing the lamp?

ask.q: You are facing the star. Are you facing the lamp? What would you have to do?
good: No. I have to turn a bit more.
The lamp is to my side.
I have to turn a little more to the left.

flow.parent: The spin and the walk must go the same way, as the real Earth spins and orbits the same way. After one turn, your child faces the star but the lamp is off to their left, about one eighth of a turn away. They must turn that bit more to face the lamp. The real Earth moves only about 1 degree a day round the Sun, not one eighth of a turn, so the extra turn is much smaller. Ask your child to point at the lamp and at the star with both arms, so they can see the angle between their arms. That angle is the extra turn.
flow.context: In this step, you turn once while moving round the lamp, as the real Earth does.

flow.do: Ask your child to turn the extra bit until they face the lamp. Then tell them the real extra turn is about 1 degree, which takes about 4 minutes.
flow.say: That extra bit is why a day is longer than one spin. For the real Earth the extra turn is about 1 degree. The Earth turns 1 degree in 4 minutes. So a day is 4 minutes longer than a spin.
flow.kid: The real extra turn is one degree. That takes four minutes.

check.q: One full spin of the Earth takes 23 hours 56 minutes. The Sun takes 24 hours to come back overhead. Why is there a gap?
options: The Earth also moves round the Sun, so it must turn a little more
The Earth spins a little faster some days
A clock hour is shorter than a real hour
check.why: While the Earth spins once, it also moves about 1 degree round the Sun. It must turn about 1 degree more, which takes about 4 minutes, to face the Sun again.

flow.context: In this step, you connect the extra turn to the 4 minutes that a day is longer than a spin.
flow.parent: Try it once more, walking the other way (clockwise). The lamp is now on the other side, so the child must turn back the other way to face it, which means less than a full day, not more. That is why the Earth's spin and its orbit going the same way makes a day longer.

flow.do: Ask your child why a star rises 4 minutes earlier each night.
flow.say: A star always lies in the same direction. After one spin, the star is back in the same place. But the Sun needs 4 minutes more. So when does the star come up, compared with yesterday?
flow.kid: Stars come back after one spin. The Sun takes four minutes more. What does that mean?
flow.parent: A star comes back after one spin, which is 4 minutes before the Sun comes back. So a star rises 4 minutes earlier each night by the clock. After 30 nights it is 2 hours earlier.
flow.think: After a whole month, how much earlier does a star rise?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Extra Turn. You link the model to what we see in the sky.

activities.title: Night Watch: who is awake while we sleep?

materials.item: a balcony, terrace, open window or the compound of your building
a torch, with red cellophane, a red polythene bag or a thick red cloth held over it with a rubber band (see the shopping list)
a notebook and a pencil
a grown-up to come along

activities.safety: A grown-up must come, and stay in a safe place away from the edge of a terrace. Do not go near wild animals. Do not touch bats, snakes or scorpions. Cover arms and legs or use the grown-up's mosquito repellent, because dusk is mosquito time.

schedule.what: Go out at dusk. Listen and look. Write down what you find. Then talk about the senses the animals used.

activities.record: A table with three columns: what I heard, what I saw, and where the light came from. Add a drawing of one night creature and the sense it needs.
activities.context: In this activity, you spend 25 minutes at dusk and just after dark finding out which animals are active near your home.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up at a balcony rail at dusk, with crows flying towards a tree and a notebook in the child's hand.
setup.caption: 1. Go out with a grown-up at dusk. Sit quietly and look at the sky.

setup.art: A child holding a torch covered with red cellophane, shining on a wall where a gecko sits near a tube light and moths flutter.
setup.caption: 2. After dark, use the red torch to look at a wall near a light.

setup.art: A notebook open to a table with three columns: heard, saw, light.
setup.caption: 3. Write down what you heard, what you saw and where the light came from.

flow.do: Choose a safe place to sit, such as a balcony or the building compound. Tell your child to be quiet and still for two minutes. Do not use the torch yet.
flow.say: We are going to find out who is awake when we are going to bed. First, sit very quietly for two minutes. Just listen. Do not use the torch yet.
flow.kid: Sit still for two minutes. Just listen.
flow.parent: Go at dusk, about half an hour after sunset. Even a city balcony has life: crows flying to roost, bats flying out, crickets, geckos, moths and sometimes frogs after rain. Keep your voice low. One child with a parent: the parent keeps watch and writes. With 2 to 4 children, split the jobs: one listens, one looks at the sky, one holds the red torch, one writes the tally, and swap after each step. If you hear and see almost nothing, count that too: write 'none' and try again on a night after rain, when frogs and insects are out.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Night Watch. You settle down and let your ears wake up.

flow.do: Ask your child to listen and look at the sky for five minutes. Write down every sound and everything that moves. Make a tally mark each time, so you end with a count for each kind. Do not use the torch.
flow.say: What can you hear? What can you see in the sky? Write down everything you notice. Is anything flying?
flow.kid: Listen and look. Write down every sound and everything that moves.

ask.q: Which sounds are made by animals, and which by people or machines?

flow.parent: At dusk, small bats such as pipistrelles flutter in zigzags between buildings. They look like swallows but fly more jerkily. Crows go to roost in groups with a lot of noise. If you see nothing, listen. Crickets, frogs and owlets are usually heard before they are seen.
flow.context: In this step, you listen and look for night animals in the sky and the air.

flow.do: Use the red torch to look at a wall, a plant or the base of a streetlight. Look for geckos, moths, beetles or spiders. Count how many you see. Note where the light is coming from.
flow.say: Now use the torch with the red cover. Look at a wall near a light. What is there? Count how many creatures you see.
flow.kid: Shine the red torch near a light. Count the creatures you see.
flow.parent: Red light usually disturbs animals less than white light and does not spoil your own night vision. Do not shine the torch into the eyes of an animal. If there are no animals, look at how the light attracts insects, and note which light sources are near.

check.q: Why do we use a red torch and not a white one?
options: Red light disturbs animals and our own night vision less
Red light is brighter
White light does not work at night
check.why: Many animals are bothered by white light, and white light also makes our eyes lose their night sight for a while. Red light is gentler on both.

flow.context: In this step, you look closely at the animals that gather around lights.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw one animal they saw or heard. Then ask which sense it needs to find its way in the dark.
flow.say: Pick one night creature. Draw it. Which sense does it use to find its way in the dark?
flow.kid: Draw one night animal. Which sense does it use?

ask.q: How might an animal that is awake at night find food, if there is no light?

flow.think: Which creatures did you find near the light, and which away from it?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Night Watch. You think about the animals' senses.

activities.title: Count the Stars: how much of the sky does a city hide?

materials.item: a cardboard tube from a roll of kitchen foil or toilet paper
a balcony, terrace or window with a view of the sky at night, on a clear night
paper and a pencil
a grown-up to come along
a fist, held out at arm's length, as a backup if your tube shows no stars at all

activities.safety: A grown-up must come along when you go outside at night.

schedule.what: Count stars through a tube with the lights on, then again after 10 minutes in the dark. Compare.

activities.record: A table with the number of stars counted in the tube patch with lights on, and with lights off after 10 minutes. If you have visited a village or a dark place, add that count.
activities.context: In this activity, you count the stars you can see through a tube and find out how much the lights around you hide.

setup.art: A child at a balcony rail looking up through a cardboard tube at a patch of sky, with a lit window behind them.
setup.caption: 1. Look at one patch of sky through the tube with the lights on. Count the stars.

setup.art: The same child with the balcony lights switched off, waiting with eyes closed beside a grown-up.
setup.caption: 2. Switch off the lights and wait 10 minutes for your eyes to adjust.

setup.art: The child looking at the same patch again and writing a bigger number in the table.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the same patch again. Count again.

flow.do: On a clear night, take your child out to a place with a view of the sky. Hold the tube up so it points at a patch of sky away from any streetlight. Ask for a guess of how many stars they will see in the tube.
flow.say: Hold the tube up and look through it at a patch of dark sky. How many stars do you think you can see? And will the number change when we switch the lights off?
flow.kid: Look through the tube. How many stars will you see? Will it change in the dark?
flow.parent: Pick a patch of sky away from the Moon. If the Moon is bright, wait for a moonless night. Mark the patch by remembering a landmark near it, such as a rooftop corner. A foil-roll tube shows a very small patch, so in a bright city it may show only 0 to 5 stars. That is a real result. If you count none with the lights on, count the stars inside your fist held out at arm's length instead, which shows a bigger patch. With 2 to 4 children, give each child a tube and one patch of sky each, or have everyone count the same patch and compare numbers. Do it on a clear night. Haze, smoke or cloud will give a count that says nothing about lights, so choose another night.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Stars. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Count the stars in the tube patch with the lights on. Write the number down. Stay in the same place and point at the same patch.
flow.say: Count the stars you can see through the tube. Write the number. Remember the patch you are looking at.
flow.kid: Count the stars in the tube. Write the number.
flow.context: In this step, you count stars with the lights on.

flow.do: Switch off all the lights you can, and shield your eyes from streetlights with a hand or a hat. Wait ten minutes without looking at a screen. Then count the stars in the same patch, still in the same place with the same tube.
flow.say: Now wait ten minutes in the dark. Do not look at any screen. Your eyes slowly get better at seeing dim things. Then count again.
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes in the dark. No screens. Then count again.
flow.parent: Your eyes need 20 to 30 minutes in the dark to see at their best, and the first ten minutes already give a clear change. Expect to see several more stars the second time, but still far fewer than in a village sky.

check.q: Your child counts more stars after waiting in the dark. Why?
options: Their eyes have become better at seeing dim light
More stars have come out
The tube has grown
check.why: The stars were there the whole time. In the dark the eyes become more sensitive, so dim stars that were hidden become visible.

flow.context: In this step, you give your eyes time to adjust and count again.

flow.do: Compare the two numbers. Ask your child why the second number is bigger, and what else might hide the stars in a city.
flow.say: Which number is bigger? Why do you think the sky looks emptier in a city?
flow.kid: Compare the two numbers. Why does a city hide the stars?
flow.parent: In a city, streetlights and building lights scatter in the air and make the sky glow, so dim stars cannot be seen against it. A study in 2016 estimated that more than 80 percent of people on Earth live under skies brightened by artificial light. If you visit a village, try this again there.
flow.think: What could a village sky show that a city sky cannot?
flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Stars. You compare and explain.

activities.title: A Day on Each Planet: one second for every hour

materials.item: a phone or watch with a stopwatch
a clear space, about 2 metres across
a pen and paper to record each planet's spin time

activities.safety: Turn slowly, with arms out, in a clear space away from furniture, stairs and sharp corners. Stop if you feel dizzy and sit down.

schedule.what: Turn like the Earth, Mars and Jupiter, with one second standing for one hour. Work out what Venus would take.

activities.record: A table with the planet, its day in hours, and the seconds it takes to turn once in the game. Add Venus with its time worked out.
activities.context: In this activity, you spin on the spot at the speed of different planets, counting one second for every hour, and compare their days.

setup.art: A child standing with arms out in a clear space, a grown-up beside them holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Stand with arms out. One second stands for one hour.

setup.art: The child turning slowly to the left while the grown-up counts to 24.
setup.caption: 2. Turn once in 24 seconds. This is the Earth.

setup.art: The child turning faster, once in 10 seconds, while a picture of Jupiter is held up.
setup.caption: 3. Turn once in 10 seconds. This is Jupiter.

flow.do: Show your child the table of day lengths. Earth is 24 hours, Mars about 24.6 hours, Jupiter about 10 hours and Venus 243 days. Ask for a guess of which planet takes the longest to turn once.
flow.say: On the game clock, one second is one hour. Earth takes 24 seconds to turn once. Which planet do you think takes the longest to turn once? Why?
flow.kid: One second is one hour. Which planet turns slowest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that planet turns the slowest?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children guess that the biggest planet turns the slowest. Jupiter is the biggest and turns the fastest.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Day on Each Planet. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Ask your child to stand with arms out and turn slowly to the left. Start the stopwatch and ask them to take 24 seconds for one full turn. Write down the time they really took and how far off it was. This is the Earth. Then do Mars at about 25 seconds.
flow.say: Turn to your left, slowly. Take 24 seconds to make one full turn. That is one Earth day. Try again for Mars, which takes 25 seconds.
flow.kid: Turn to your left. Take 24 seconds for one turn. That is Earth.
flow.parent: Count aloud together. A slow, steady turn is the idea. Children turn too fast at first, so this is harder than it looks. Working together: one child turns, one runs the stopwatch and counts aloud, one writes down the real time. With 2 to 4 children everyone tries each planet and the group writes who came closest to 24 seconds for the Earth. One child with a parent can swap jobs. A good test: try the turn again with the same time, and see if you get better. Do not spin faster than the target time, because the aim is slow and steady.
flow.context: In this step, you spin at the speed of the Earth and Mars.

flow.do: Now ask your child to turn once in only 10 seconds. This is Jupiter. Ask how it feels different from the Earth turn.
flow.say: Now turn once in 10 seconds. That is Jupiter. It spins more than twice in one Earth day. How does it feel?
flow.kid: Turn once in ten seconds. That is Jupiter. How does it feel?

ask.q: Jupiter is much bigger than the Earth. How can it turn faster?
good: It was spun fast when it formed.
It formed from a fast-spinning cloud.

flow.parent: Jupiter is mostly gas and is bigger than 1,000 Earths in volume. It spins once in about 9 hours 56 minutes. Its middle is carried at more than 40,000 kilometres an hour. Scientists think the planets got their spin from the swirling cloud they formed from.
flow.context: In this step, you spin at the speed of Jupiter, the fastest big planet.

flow.do: Ask your child to work out Venus. Venus takes 243 Earth days to turn once. One Earth day is 24 seconds in the game. Multiply 243 by 24 seconds. Change the answer to minutes.
flow.say: Venus takes 243 Earth days to turn once. One Earth day is 24 seconds in our game. How many seconds would Venus take to turn once? How many minutes is that?
flow.kid: Venus takes 243 days to turn. Each day is 24 seconds. Work it out.
flow.parent: 243 times 24 is 5,832 seconds. 5,832 divided by 60 is about 97 minutes. So Venus would take about an hour and a half to turn once. Venus spins the opposite way to the Earth, so the Sun would rise in the west.
flow.think: Venus turns backwards. If you turned the other way, what would the Sun do?
flow.context: This is the last step of A Day on Each Planet. You work out how long Venus would take in the game.

activities.title: The Clock Debate: should India have one time zone or two?

materials.item: a map of India, drawn or printed, with Guwahati and Mumbai marked
four role cards written on paper, one for each speaker
paper and a pencil to keep a tally of votes

schedule.what: Read the facts. Each person speaks for their role. Vote, then say whether anyone changed their mind.

activities.record: The vote before and after the debate, and one sentence on each role's best reason.
activities.context: In this activity, you take the parts of different people and argue about whether India should keep one clock for the whole country, or have two.

setup.art: A family sitting round a table with a map of India and four role cards placed in front of them.
setup.caption: 1. Sit round the map. Give out the four role cards.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says tea planter in Assam and pointing at Guwahati on the map.
setup.caption: 2. Each person speaks for the person on their card.

setup.art: The family raising hands for a vote, with a tally on paper.
setup.caption: 3. Vote at the end. Did anyone change their mind?

flow.do: Read the facts together. India has one clock, Indian Standard Time. The Sun is highest about an hour earlier in the far east than in the middle. In the far west it is about an hour later. Vote now: one time zone or two?
flow.say: India uses one clock. In the far east, the Sun rises very early. In the far west, it rises much later by the same clock. Should India have one time zone or two? Vote now, before we talk.
flow.kid: India has one clock. Should it have one zone or two? Vote now.
flow.parent: Write the first vote down. The roles are: a tea planter in Assam, a railway timetable planner, a Class 4 child in Arunachal Pradesh who walks home from school in winter, and a shopkeeper in Gujarat. Some Assam tea gardens already keep their own garden time, one hour ahead of Indian Standard Time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clock Debate. You vote before you hear the arguments.

flow.do: Give each person a role card. Each one speaks for one minute for their role, then all four may ask each other questions. The planner worries about confusion. The child worries about walking home from school in the dark.
flow.say: Each of us speaks for one minute as the person on the card. Say what you would gain or lose. Then we may ask each other questions.
flow.kid: Speak for one minute as your role. What would you gain or lose?

ask.q: What would change for the railway planner if there were two zones?
good: Trains crossing the border would need a clock change.

ask.q: What would change for the child in Arunachal Pradesh?
good: Sunset would come an hour later by the clock.

flow.parent: There is no right answer. People disagree for good reasons. A single clock is simple, and a zone for the east follows the Sun more closely. Do not steer the vote. Only one child: the child picks two roles and the parent plays the other two, speaking in turn. With 2 to 4 children, give out one role card each and let any extra children be the judges who keep the tally of arguments for each side. Four cards can be written in a minute on scrap paper.
flow.context: In this step, you argue from different points of view.

flow.do: Vote again. Count the votes. Ask if anyone changed their mind, and which argument changed it. Then ask what facts about the Sun would help decide.
flow.say: Vote again. Did anyone change their mind? What changed it?
flow.kid: Vote again. Did anyone change their mind? Why?
flow.parent: A good result is that your child can name one reason for each side. The Sun's time belongs to each place. The clock is an agreement among people. The question is how much to bend one to suit the other.
flow.think: Is a clock supposed to follow the Sun, or to help people work together?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Clock Debate. You vote again and think about what you learned.

projects.title: Star Gate: the star that comes early

materials.item: a window, balcony or terrace with a view of a clear patch of sky in the west, and a fixed edge at least a fist's width (about 10 degrees) above the horizon, such as a rooftop corner or a water tank
a piece of tape to mark exactly where your eye must be
a watch, clock or phone that shows the time to the minute
a notebook and a pencil
a grown-up to come along

projects.safety: A grown-up must come along when you watch at night, and stay with the child. On a terrace, stay well back from the open edge. Use mosquito repellent or cover your arms and legs.

schedule.what: Choose the spot, the edge and a bright star. Write the time the star goes behind the edge.
Same spot. Write the time again.
Same spot. Write the time again.
Same spot. Write the time again.
Same spot. Write the time again.
Compare all the times and explain.

projects.record: A table with the night, the time the star went behind the edge, and how many minutes earlier than night 1. Draw a line graph of the times.
projects.context: In this project, you watch the same star go behind the same edge on several nights and find out how many minutes earlier it goes each night.

setup.art: A child standing on a balcony with a piece of tape on the floor where their feet go, looking at a bright star just above a rooftop corner.
setup.caption: 1. Mark your spot with tape. Choose a bright star near a fixed edge.

setup.art: A notebook with a table: night 1 to night 6, the time the star vanished and the minutes earlier.
setup.caption: 2. Each night, write the time the star goes behind the edge.

setup.art: A line graph with six points sloping downwards, one for each night.
setup.caption: 3. At the end, draw a graph of your six times.

flow.do: Find a place with a fixed edge in the west, such as a rooftop or a tree. Pick a bright star about to go behind it. Mark where your eyes are with tape. Write down the exact time the star disappears.
flow.say: Pick a bright star in the western sky that is about to go behind a rooftop or a tree. Stand on the tape mark. Write down the exact minute the star disappears.
flow.kid: Pick a bright star near an edge. Stand on the tape. Write the time it vanishes.

ask.q: Do you think the star will vanish at the same time tomorrow? Why do you think so?
good: Yes, because the Earth turns once a day.
No, because the Earth moves round the Sun.

flow.parent: Choose a star, not a planet. Stars twinkle. Planets shine with a steady light and move against the stars. The Moon will not work, because it moves too fast. Start watching about 20 minutes before the star disappears. Stay in the same exact spot each night, because moving a metre changes the time. The Stellarium Web planetarium can help you find a bright star. If the time hardly changes from night to night, less than 2 minutes, you have picked a planet, so choose a different star. Stars near the horizon fade in haze, so a high edge works better. No phone? Ask which bright 'star' in the west at dusk is a planet, or pick the brightest one that twinkles. One child with a parent: the child stands on the tape and calls 'gone', and the parent reads the watch and writes. With 2 to 4 children, take turns on the tape, one standing, one with the watch and one writing, and swap each night. Only one pair of eyes should stand on the tape each night, so everyone sees the same thing.

check.q: Why do we stand in exactly the same spot each night?
options: So the only thing that changes is the date
So the star looks bigger
Because the star can see us
check.why: The star's position against the edge depends on where our eyes are. If we move, we change the result. A fair test changes only one thing.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Star Gate. You choose your spot and record the first night.

flow.do: Next night, go to the same spot at the same time as before, minus about 10 minutes. Write down the exact time the star disappears behind the same edge.
flow.say: Go back to the tape mark tonight. Watch the same star. Write the exact time it vanishes. Is it earlier or later than yesterday?
flow.kid: Go back to the tape. Watch the same star. Write the time it vanishes.
flow.parent: Expect the star to vanish about 4 minutes earlier than on night 1. If cloud stopped you on one night, the next gap will be about twice as big. That is normal.
flow.wait: Do this on the next clear night.
flow.context: In this step, you record the second night.

flow.do: On each of the next three clear nights, go to the same spot and write down the exact time the star disappears. Write down how many minutes earlier it is than night 1.
flow.say: Do the same on the next three clear nights. Each time, subtract the time from night 1. How many minutes earlier is it?
flow.kid: Repeat for three more nights. Subtract from night 1 each time.
flow.parent: If the star hides behind a cloud, miss that night. Your table still works. A gap of two nights should give about 8 minutes.
flow.wait: Do this on the next three clear nights.
flow.context: In this step, you record three more nights.

flow.do: Draw a line graph of the times, with the night along the bottom and the minutes earlier up the side. Ask your child to explain the pattern.
flow.say: Plot your times as a line graph. What pattern do you see? Why does the star vanish earlier each night?
flow.kid: Plot a line graph. What pattern do you see? Why?
flow.parent: Expect a straight line sloping down, at about 4 minutes a night. Typical numbers: after 5 nights, night 5 is about 16 minutes earlier than night 1 (four gaps of about 4 minutes). The star comes back to the same place after one spin, which is 23 hours 56 minutes. The Sun takes 24 hours. So the star keeps 4 minutes ahead of the clock. After a month, it is 2 hours earlier. After a year, it is back to the start. If you cannot see stars at all, use the Stellarium Web planetarium on a phone, and step the date forward one day at a time.
flow.think: After a whole month, how much earlier would the star vanish? Where would it be at the same time of night?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Star Gate. You graph your results and explain them.

challenges.title: Plan the Family Call: find a time that suits four places
challenges.problem: Your family in Chennai wants one video call with four relatives. One is in Dubai, one in London, one in Singapore and one in Tokyo. Everyone should be called between 8 in the morning and 8 in the evening their own time. Your own school finishes at 3 in the afternoon, so the call must start after that. Find a start time in Chennai that works for all five places.
constraints: Use the clock differences in the table. Dubai is 1 hour 30 minutes behind Chennai. London is 5 hours 30 minutes behind Chennai in winter. Singapore is 2 hours 30 minutes ahead of Chennai. Tokyo is 3 hours 30 minutes ahead of Chennai.
Every person must be called between 8 in the morning and 8 in the evening, their own time.
The call must start at or after 3 in the afternoon in Chennai.
Write your answer as a start time in Chennai and the matching time in each of the other four places.
materials: a paper clock face, or a real clock, to help count hours
general: Work out the earliest and the latest start time for each place, then find the times that all five places allow.
Pick 4 in the afternoon in Chennai, and check each place.
creative: Draw five strips of paper, one for each place, and slide them against each other to see where the awake hours overlap.
Draw five clock faces in a row and shade each place's allowed hours in a colour, then find the colour overlap.
challenges.your_turn: Choose any four places in the world, look up their time differences from Chennai, and find a call time that suits all of them. Is there always a good time? What would you do if there was none?
challenges.context: This is a challenge about clock times in different places. You use your knowledge of how clocks follow the Sun to plan a call.

setup.art: A table showing four cities and how many hours ahead or behind Chennai each one is.
setup.caption: 1. Read the table of clock differences.

setup.art: Five paper strips laid side by side, each showing the allowed hours for one city, with the overlap shaded.
setup.caption: 2. Find the hours that every place allows.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Make sure your child knows what ahead and behind mean. Ask them to guess if a good time exists.
flow.say: A place that is ahead of Chennai has a later time on its clock. A place that is behind has an earlier time. Will there be a time that suits all five places?
flow.kid: Ahead means a later time. Behind means an earlier time. Is there a good call time?
flow.parent: Check that your child understands the direction. When it is 3 in the afternoon in Chennai, it is 1:30 in the afternoon in Dubai and 9:30 in the morning in London. Singapore is 5:30 in the evening, and Tokyo is 6:30 in the evening.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plan the Family Call challenge. You read the problem and guess.

flow.do: For each city, work out the earliest and latest Chennai time that suits it. Write them down. Look for the times that all five allow.
flow.say: For each city, find the earliest and latest time in Chennai that works. For London, 8 in the morning there is 1:30 in the afternoon in Chennai. Do the other cities.
flow.kid: For each city, find the earliest and latest time in Chennai that works.
flow.parent: London: 8 in the morning there is 1:30 pm in Chennai, and 8 in the evening there is 1:30 am. Tokyo: 8 in the evening there is 4:30 pm in Chennai. Singapore: 8 in the evening there is 5:30 pm. Dubai: 8 in the evening there is 9:30 pm. School ends at 3. So the call can start between 3 pm and 4:30 pm in Chennai.

check.q: Tokyo is 3 hours 30 minutes ahead of Chennai. It is 8 in the evening in Tokyo. What time is it in Chennai?
options: 4:30 in the afternoon
11:30 in the evening
12:30 in the afternoon
check.why: Tokyo is ahead, so Chennai is behind. 8 in the evening minus 3 hours 30 minutes is 4:30 in the afternoon.

flow.context: In this step, you work out the allowed times in Chennai for each place.

flow.do: Choose a start time in Chennai, and write down the time in each place. Check that nobody is called too early or too late.
flow.say: Pick a start time. Write the time in all five places. Is anyone too early or too late?
flow.kid: Pick a start time. Write the time in each place. Check each one.
flow.parent: Any start time between 3 pm and 4:30 pm in Chennai works. At 3:30 pm: Dubai is 2 pm, London is 10 am, Singapore is 6 pm and Tokyo is 7 pm. A good discussion point is why Singapore's clock is about an hour ahead of its Sun time. Clock times are agreements, and countries choose them for many reasons.
flow.think: Which place made the plan hardest, and why?
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge. You choose a time and check it.

challenges.title: Dark-Sky Street Lamp: light the road, not the sky
challenges.problem: Design a street lamp from a torch and a few things from the kitchen drawer that lights the road below it but sends almost no light up into the sky or sideways into a nearby house. Test it in a dark room.
constraints: The lamp must be a torch, or a phone torch, held 30 centimetres above the table.
You may use paper, card, a paper cup, black paper and tape. You may not turn the torch off.
A white card held 20 centimetres above the lamp stands for the sky. A second card held at the side stands for a window.
Test in a dark room, with a grown-up. Judge by eye which card is brighter.
materials: a torch or a phone torch
a paper cup, paper, card and black paper
general: A paper cup over the torch with the open end facing down, so the light goes only downwards.
A cone of black paper round the torch that points down at the road.
creative: A cup with a small hole cut in the bottom, so that the light makes a small bright circle on the road.
A lamp that is lower and has a flat top, so less light spills sideways.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it with the sky card and the window card. Change one thing and test again. Which design put the most light on the road and the least on the cards? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about light pollution. You build a lamp that lights the ground but not the sky.

setup.art: A torch taped to a pencil standing in a lump of clay on a table, with a white card held above it and a second card beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Set up the bare torch with a sky card above and a window card at the side.

setup.art: The same torch with a paper cup over it, open end down, with the cards much darker.
setup.caption: 2. Add a shade and compare the cards again.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the bare torch with the two cards in a dark room. Ask which card is brighter.
flow.say: This is a street lamp with no shade. In a dark room, look at the sky card and the window card. Which one is brighter? What does the bare lamp do?
flow.kid: Look at the bare torch in the dark. Which card is brighter?
flow.parent: A bare lamp lights everything, including the sky card and the window card. Do not shine the torch at anyone's face.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dark-Sky Street Lamp challenge. You look at a lamp with no shade.

flow.do: Build a shade. Try a paper cup with the open end down. Test with both cards. Then try a second shade. Write which shade lit the road best and the cards least.
flow.say: Make a shade for the lamp. Try a paper cup, open end down. Look at both cards. Now try a different shade. Which is better?
flow.kid: Build a shade. Look at both cards. Try a second shade.
flow.parent: The cup stops light going up and sideways. Lit properly, the table below should be bright and the cards dark. Light is also scattered by the air, but in a model this is small. If the torch gets hot, let it cool.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test two shades.

flow.do: Choose your best shade. Show it to a grown-up. Explain why it is better for turtles, stars and neighbours.
flow.say: Which shade was best? Why? Who benefits from a lamp that sends light down?
flow.kid: Which shade was best? Who benefits from it?
flow.parent: Real dark-sky lamps work the same way: a shield stops light going upwards, and warm-coloured, dimmer light disturbs animals less. Lights that point down use less electricity for the same brightness on the ground.
flow.think: What is a lamp for? Who is it for?
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge. You choose your best lamp and explain why.

worksheets.title: Day and Night, Noon and Speed (core)

items.p: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. How long does it take to turn 1 degree?
opts: 4 minutes
15 minutes
1 minute
items.why: 24 hours is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 360 is 4. So the Earth turns 1 degree every 4 minutes.

items.p: Seen from above the North Pole, which way does the Earth spin?
opts: Anticlockwise, from west to east
Clockwise, from east to west
It does not spin, and the Sun goes round it
items.why: The Earth turns from west to east. That is why the Sun seems to rise in the east and why places in the east see the Sun first.

items.p: City A is 5 degrees of longitude west of city B. When is the Sun at its highest in A, compared with B?
opts: About 20 minutes later
About 20 minutes earlier
At the same time
items.why: 5 degrees times 4 minutes is 20 minutes. A is to the west, so the Sun reaches it later.

items.p: At 12 o'clock on the clock, the Sun is at its highest in every city in India.
items.why: False. Everyone uses one clock, but the Sun is highest about 4 minutes later for every degree you go west. In Guwahati it is about 37 minutes before 12 and in Mumbai about 38 minutes after.

items.p: The Sun is at its highest about ____ minutes later for every degree of longitude we go west.
items.why: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 1,440 minutes, which is 4 minutes for each degree.

items.p: A town has sunrise at 6:20 in the morning and sunset at 18:00. At what time is the Sun at its highest? Write it as hours and minutes, like 12:10.
items.why: From 6:20 to 18:00 is 11 hours 40 minutes. Half is 5 hours 50 minutes. 6:20 plus 5:50 is 12:10.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: how far north or south of the equator a place is
how far east or west of Greenwich a place is
the circle around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the poles
the line the Earth spins around
items.why: Latitude tells you how far north or south you are. Longitude tells you how far east or west. The equator is halfway between the poles. The axis is the line that the Earth turns about.

items.p: Put these cities in the order in which the Sun rises over them, first to last: Mumbai, Dong, Chennai, Guwahati.
items.why: The Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun reaches the places in the east first. Dong is furthest east, then Guwahati, then Chennai, and Mumbai is furthest west.

items.p: A circle drawn on a spinning ball is shorter near the pole than at the equator. Why does that make a spot near the pole move more slowly?
opts: It goes round a shorter path in the same time
It is further from the Sun
It is colder there
items.why: Every spot goes round once in 24 hours. A shorter path in the same time means a slower speed.

items.p: A person standing at the North Pole is carried round at about 1,670 kilometres an hour.
items.why: False. A person at the pole only turns on the spot. The speed of about 1,670 kilometres an hour belongs to the equator.

items.p: Why can we not feel the Earth spinning?
opts: It turns smoothly and steadily, and we are carried along with everything around us
It is too slow to be real
We feel it, but we get used to it
items.why: A smooth, steady motion cannot be felt. We feel bumps, starts and stops, like in a train. Everything around us is carried along too.

items.p: The Earth is a little wider across the ____ than from pole to pole, because it spins.
items.why: The spin flings the Earth outward a little around its middle. The difference is about 43 kilometres.

items.p: Meera says: 'All the clocks in India say 12, so the Sun must be highest everywhere at the same moment.' Explain in one or two sentences why she is wrong.
items.a: The clock is an agreement. The Sun is highest about 4 minutes later for every degree you go west, so it is highest earlier in the east and later in the west.
items.why: A strong answer says that one clock is shared, but the Sun's position depends on where you are, and gives the 4 minutes for each degree rule.

items.p: A child draws a circle on a ball at the equator and another at 60 degrees north. Which circle is longer, and what does that tell you about how fast a spot on each circle is carried?
items.a: The circle at the equator is longer, about twice as long. A spot on it goes about twice as fast, because it has further to go in the same time.
items.why: A strong answer says the equator circle is longer and, since every spot turns once in a day, a longer circle means a faster spot.

items.p: Draw the Earth from above the North Pole with the Sun on one side. Shade the night half. Mark where it is sunrise, and draw an arrow for the way the Earth turns.
items.a: A circle for the Earth with the Sun to one side, the far half shaded, an anticlockwise arrow, and sunrise marked on the line between night and day on the side where the Earth is turning into the light.
items.why: A strong drawing shows half the Earth lit and half dark, an anticlockwise arrow, and sunrise at the edge where the ground is turning from dark into light.

items.p: A plane flies from Port Blair, at about 93 degrees east, to Chennai, at about 80 degrees east. By how many minutes is the Sun's highest moment later in Chennai?
items.why: 93 minus 80 is 13 degrees. 13 times 4 is 52 minutes.

items.p: Two cities are on almost the same line of longitude, but one is much further north. When is the Sun highest in each?
opts: At almost the same clock time
Much earlier in the northern city
Much later in the northern city
items.why: Noon depends on longitude only. Cities on the same line of longitude have their Sun at its highest at the same time, however far north or south they are.

items.p: The gaps between sunrise times of different cities are untidy, but the gaps between noons are neat. Why?
opts: Sunrise also depends on how far north a city is and on the season, but noon depends only on longitude
Noon is easier to measure
Sunrise depends on the clock but noon does not
items.why: Winter sunrises come later in the north and summer sunrises come earlier. Noon is the middle of the day, and that middle depends only on how far east or west you are.

items.p: The Earth spins once in exactly 24 hours.
items.why: False. One spin takes 23 hours 56 minutes. The day from one noon to the next is 24 hours, because the Earth also moves round the Sun.

items.p: Why does a bright star rise about 4 minutes earlier each night?
opts: The star is back after one spin, which is 4 minutes before the Sun is back
The star moves closer to us each night
Our clocks run slow
items.why: A star returns after one spin of 23 hours 56 minutes. The clock day is 24 hours. So the star keeps 4 minutes ahead of the clock each night.

items.p: One full spin of the Earth, compared with the stars, takes 23 hours and ____ minutes.
items.why: One spin takes 23 hours 56 minutes. The extra 4 minutes to make a 24-hour day come from the Earth moving round the Sun.

items.p: A person on the equator is carried round the Earth, a distance of 40,000 kilometres, in 24 hours. About how many kilometres in one hour, to the nearest 10?
items.why: 40,000 divided by 24 is about 1,667. To the nearest 10, that is 1,670 kilometres.

items.p: At 60 degrees north, the circle is half as long as the equator. About how many kilometres an hour is a person there carried, if the equator speed is 1,670?
items.why: Half of 1,670 is 835. The same turn in the same time on a path half as long means half the speed.

items.p: Sort each statement into the group where it belongs.
items: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours
Noon comes about 4 minutes later for each degree west
The Earth's day is slowly getting longer
Whether India should have two time zones
items.why: The spin, the 4-minutes rule and the slowing day are backed by measurements. The cause of the moths' circling, the reason for Venus's backward spin and the question of two time zones are still argued.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Venus. Think about the length of each planet's day compared with its year.
items.a: Venus. Its day (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days). For the other three, a day is much shorter than a year.
items.why: Venus spins so slowly that one spin takes longer than one trip round the Sun. This is true of no other planet in this list.

items.p: What is slowing the Earth's spin?
opts: The Moon's pull on the oceans, which makes tides that rub on the sea floor
The Earth is running out of energy from the Sun
The wind blowing against the ground
items.why: The tides raised by the Moon move over the sea floor and rub like a gentle brake. The Earth loses spin energy, and the Moon gains some and moves slowly away.

items.p: Fossil corals that lived about 400 million years ago show about 400 daily growth lines in each year. What does this suggest?
opts: A year had about 400 days, so each day was shorter than today's
The year was longer than it is today
Corals grow faster than they used to
items.why: The length of a year has stayed about the same. If a year had about 400 days, each day was about 22 hours long.

items.p: A barn owl finds a mouse in the dark mainly by her ears. What helps her work out where the sound is coming from?
opts: Her ears sit at different heights, so the sound reaches them at slightly different times
She has one very large ear
She hears best when she closes her eyes
items.why: Her left and right ears hear the rustle at tiny different moments and loudness. Her brain uses the difference to find the direction and the height.

items.p: Streetlights on a beach can lead baby turtles away from the sea.
items.why: True. Hatchlings crawl towards the brightest, lowest horizon, which on a dark natural beach is the open sea. Streetlights can fool them.

items.p: Explain, using the idea of a smaller circle, why a person at the North Pole is not carried at 1,670 kilometres an hour.
items.a: At the pole, the circle you travel round has no length, so you only turn on the spot. A smaller circle covered in the same 24 hours means a lower speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the path gets shorter as you go north, so the speed gets smaller, and at the pole it is zero.

items.p: The Sun is highest in Dwarka, at 69 degrees east, at 12:40 by the clock. What time is it highest in Kohima, at 94 degrees east?
items.why: Kohima is 25 degrees east of Dwarka. 25 times 4 is 100 minutes, which is 1 hour 40 minutes. The Sun is highest in Kohima earlier, at 12:40 minus 1:40, which is 11:00.

items.p: Draw a globe with a circle at the equator and a circle at 60 degrees north. Draw arrows to show which place is carried faster, and write how many times faster.
items.a: A globe with two circles, a long one at the equator and a half-length one near the top, longer arrow on the equator, and the label 2 times faster.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the equator circle about twice as long as the 60 degree circle, so the equator's arrow is about twice as long.

items.p: Two friends are talking about school start times in a state in the far east of India, where the Sun rises very early.

views.who: Isha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: School should start at the same clock time everywhere in the country. A shared clock keeps things fair and simple.

views.who: Arjun, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: School in the east should start earlier by the clock. The Sun rises much earlier there, and we should use the morning light.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What facts about the Sun and the clock would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and uses a fact such as noon being about 58 minutes earlier in Dong than at the middle of India.
items.why: Both views have a point. A single clock is simple, and following the Sun saves daylight. The clock is an agreement and the Sun's time belongs to each place.

worksheets.title: Clocks, Noon and the Slowing Earth (challenge)

items.p: One town is at 85 degrees east and another is at 71 degrees east. The Sun is highest in the first at 11:50. At what time is it highest in the second? Show your working.
items.why: The second town is 14 degrees west. 14 times 4 is 56 minutes. 11:50 plus 56 minutes is 12:46.

items.p: Indian Standard Time matches the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. A town is 7.5 degrees west of that line. At what clock time is the Sun highest there?
items.why: 7.5 times 4 is 30 minutes. West means later, so the Sun is highest at 12:30.

items.p: A town is 11 degrees east of the 82.5 degrees east line. At what clock time is the Sun highest there?
items.why: 11 times 4 is 44 minutes. East means earlier, so the Sun is highest at 12:00 minus 44 minutes, which is 11:16.

items.p: Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of world time (UTC). Why this number?
opts: It matches the Sun at 82.5 degrees east, and 82.5 divided by 15 is 5.5
It was chosen because it is easy to remember
India is 5.5 hours from the Sun
items.why: The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. 82.5 degrees east is 5.5 hours of turning ahead of Greenwich, so the Sun reaches it 5 hours 30 minutes earlier.

items.p: A jet flying west near 60 degrees north goes about 835 kilometres an hour, the same as the ground's spin speed there. What would passengers see of the Sun's height in the sky?
opts: It would stay at nearly the same height for a long time
The Sun would set faster than on the ground
The Sun would rise in the west
items.why: The plane moves west as fast as the ground is carried east. So it stays under the same part of the sky, and the Sun hardly moves.

items.p: Which statement about Venus is true?
opts: One spin takes longer than one trip round the Sun, and it spins backwards
It spins faster than any other planet
It has a day of exactly 24 hours
items.why: Venus spins once in 243 Earth days and goes round the Sun in 225 Earth days. It also spins the opposite way, so the Sun would rise in the west.

items.p: Fossil corals show that the Earth's days were longer 400 million years ago than they are today.
items.why: False. Corals with about 400 daily lines in a year show that a year had about 400 days, so each day was shorter, about 22 hours.

items.p: Suppose a day gets 2 thousandths of a second (0.002 seconds) longer every hundred years, and keeps doing so. How many seconds longer is a day after 10,000 hundred-year periods, which is a million years?
items.why: 10,000 times 0.002 is 20 seconds. The real rate changes with time, but it shows how small steps add up.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? An owl's ears, a bat's echoes, a python's heat pits, a cricket's ears.
items.a: The python's heat pits. The other three work by hearing, and the pits feel warmth.
items.why: The owl, the bat and the cricket all find things by hearing. The python senses the warmth of her prey, which is a different sense.

items.p: Too much artificial light at night, which hides stars and confuses animals, is called light ____.
items.why: Light pollution is light in the wrong place or at the wrong time. It hides the stars and can lead turtles, birds and insects astray.

items.p: Put these in order to explain why a day is 24 hours when one spin takes 23 hours 56 minutes.
a: The Earth spins once, and a faraway star is back in the same place
The Earth has also moved about 1 degree along its path round the Sun
The Earth must turn about 1 degree more to face the Sun again
That extra turn takes about 4 minutes, so the day is 24 hours
items.why: After a full spin, a faraway star is in the same place. But the Earth has moved a little round the Sun, so the Sun is not yet back. The extra turn of about 1 degree takes about 4 minutes.

items.p: Match each finding to the evidence behind it.
pairs: The Earth is wider at the equator than from pole to pole
Surveyors found that a degree of latitude is longer near the pole
Growth lines on fossil corals and records of ancient eclipses
Noon comes later in the west
Sunrise and sunset tables for cities at different longitudes
Light at night harms turtle hatchlings
Studies of hatchlings crawling on lit and dark beaches
items.why: Each finding was shown by a different kind of measurement. Good evidence matches the claim it supports.

items.p: Give one reason why a country might keep one clock time, and one reason why it might want more than one.
items.a: One clock keeps timetables, banks and phones simple. Two zones follow the Sun better, so people in the far east or far west would have more useful daylight.
items.why: A strong answer gives a fair reason for each side and shows that the choice is about people's needs, not about nature.

items.p: A friend says: 'Noon is a fact about the Sun, not about clocks.' Do you agree? Use two cities to explain.
items.a: I agree. The Sun is highest at about 11:23 in Guwahati and 12:38 in Mumbai. The Sun's noon belongs to each place. The clock says 12 in both, but that is an agreement.
items.why: A strong answer separates the Sun's highest point, which depends on place, from the clock's 12 o'clock, which people agreed, and uses two cities as evidence.

items.p: Draw the Earth and the Moon. Use arrows to show how the Moon's pull on the tides slows the Earth's spin.
items.a: The Earth with a bulge of ocean towards the Moon, an arrow for the Earth's spin, and an arrow showing the tide dragging against the spin. The Moon is drawn a little further away.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the tide bulge, the Earth's spin and the tide rubbing against it like a brake.

items.p: A town on the coast wants brighter lights on its beach for safety. Turtle watchers say the lights confuse the hatchlings.

views.who: Priya, a town councillor (an imagined view)
views.says: Bright lights keep people safe at night and make the beach pleasant. We should put in more lights.

views.who: Farhan, a turtle watcher (an imagined view)
views.says: Hatchlings use the brightest horizon to find the sea. We should use dim, shielded lights, and switch them off in hatching season.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? Is there a way to give people safety and also protect the turtles?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side or finds a middle way, such as shielded lights that point down, lights that are warm in colour, or lights that switch off in hatching season, and gives a reason.
items.why: Both safety and wildlife matter. Shielded, dim lights that point at the ground show how a design can help both.

quiz.p: Two cities are 10 degrees of longitude apart, and city B is to the west of city A. By about how much later is the Sun at its highest in city B?
opts: 40 minutes
10 minutes
100 minutes
quiz.why: 10 degrees times 4 minutes is 40 minutes. B is to the west, so the Sun reaches it later.

quiz.p: Sunrise is at 5:40 and sunset is at 18:20. When is the Sun at its highest?
quiz.why: From 5:40 to 18:20 is 12 hours 40 minutes. Half is 6 hours 20 minutes. 5:40 plus 6:20 is 12:00.

quiz.p: Why is a person at 60 degrees north carried more slowly than a person on the equator?
opts: Their circle is shorter, and they go round it in the same 24 hours
They are further from the Sun
The Earth turns more slowly there
quiz.why: Every place turns once in 24 hours. A shorter circle in the same time means a slower speed. A wrong answer that the Earth turns more slowly there would mean the day is longer there, which it is not.

quiz.p: All of India uses one clock, but the Sun is highest at different moments in different cities. Why do we use one clock?
opts: It is an agreement that makes timetables and communication simple
The Sun is highest at the same time everywhere
The Earth stops spinning at the borders
quiz.why: Indian Standard Time is set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east and used for the whole country. The Sun's own time is different in each place.

quiz.p: One spin of the Earth takes 23 hours 56 minutes, but a day is 24 hours. Why the 4 extra minutes?
opts: The Earth also moves round the Sun, so it must turn a little more to face the Sun again
The Earth slows down at night
Clocks are set wrongly
quiz.why: After one spin the Earth has moved about 1 degree round the Sun. It needs about 1 degree more of turning, which takes about 4 minutes.

quiz.p: What is the main reason the Earth's days are slowly getting longer?
opts: Tides raised by the Moon act as a gentle brake
The wind blows against the spin
The Sun's heat slows the Earth
quiz.why: As the tides move over the sea floor, they rub and take energy from the Earth's spin.

quiz.p: A day on Jupiter lasts about 10 Earth hours. About how many Jupiter days fit into one Earth day of 24 hours?
opts: A little more than 2
A little more than 1
About 10
quiz.why: 24 divided by 10 is 2.4. So Jupiter turns a little more than 2 times in an Earth day.

quiz.p: Why can streetlights on a beach harm baby turtles?
opts: They crawl towards the brightest horizon, and a streetlight can be brighter than the sea
They are scared of the light
The light is too warm for them
quiz.why: Hatchlings use the bright, low horizon to find the sea. A road light can fool them into walking the wrong way.

quiz.p: Which night animal finds prey mainly by sensing warmth?
opts: An Indian rock python
A barn owl
A bat
quiz.why: A python has heat-sensing pits on her lips. An owl and a bat find prey mainly by hearing.

quiz.p: At 12 noon on the clock, which statement about Guwahati and Mumbai is true?
opts: The Sun has already passed its highest in Guwahati and has not yet reached it in Mumbai
The Sun is at its highest in both
The Sun is at its highest in Mumbai before Guwahati
quiz.why: Guwahati is in the east, so its noon comes earlier, about 11:23. Mumbai's noon comes later, about 12:38.

quiz.p: The Earth is a little wider across the equator than from pole to pole, because it spins.
quiz.why: True. The spin makes the Earth bulge at its middle. The difference is about 43 kilometres.

quiz.p: A town is 4 degrees east of the line at 82.5 degrees east, where the Sun is highest at 12:00. When is the Sun highest in that town?
opts: 16 minutes before 12:00
16 minutes after 12:00
Exactly at 12:00
quiz.why: 4 times 4 is 16 minutes. East means earlier, so the Sun is highest at 11:44.

applications: Railway and flight timetables, which all use a single agreed clock time across places where the Sun's time differs.
