open_questions.q: Why does Venus spin backwards, so slowly that its day is longer than its year?
open_questions.why_open: Ideas include a giant crash long ago, and the pull of the Sun on its thick air. Nobody has shown which is right.

open_questions.q: How fast was the Earth spinning when it was young, and how long was the first day?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree it was much faster. The numbers depend on how the Moon formed, and that is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why do moths and other insects circle lights?
open_questions.why_open: Studies in 2024 gave a new explanation, that insects tilt their backs towards the light. More experiments are needed to test it.

open_questions.q: Is there a 'now' that is the same everywhere in the universe?
open_questions.why_open: Einstein's relativity says that 'at the same time' depends on how observers move. What this means for the universe as a whole is still discussed.

open_questions.q: What exactly made the Earth spin in the first place?
open_questions.why_open: The planets formed from a swirling cloud, but the details of how the Earth got its spin, and how a giant crash changed it, are still argued.

maths.problem: In Kochi, a child finds sunrise at 6:14 in the morning and sunset at 17:58. When is noon?
maths.explain: From 6:14 to 17:58 is 11 hours 44 minutes. Half of 11 hours 44 minutes is 5 hours 52 minutes. 6:14 plus 5:52 is 12:06.
maths.context: In the Five Noons test, you find noon for each city from its sunrise and sunset times. These are made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Halving the time between sunrise and sunset gives noon, which depends only on longitude. Working in hours and minutes shows how a clock measures the Sun.

maths.problem: Chennai is at 80 degrees east and Kochi is at 76 degrees east. The Earth turns 1 degree in 4 minutes. By how many minutes does the Sun's highest moment differ?
maths.explain: 80 minus 76 is 4 degrees. 4 times 4 is 16 minutes. Chennai is the more eastern, so its noon is 16 minutes earlier.
maths.context: In the Five Noons test, you find that noon shifts by 4 minutes for each degree of longitude.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the gap in degrees by 4 turns a map distance into a time difference, so you can predict noons without looking them up.

maths.problem: The Sun reaches the line at 82.5 degrees east 5 hours 30 minutes before it reaches Greenwich. The Earth turns 15 degrees each hour. Check this: what is 82.5 divided by 15?
maths.explain: 15 times 5 is 75. There are 7.5 left. Half of 15 is 7.5, so that is half an hour more. 82.5 divided by 15 is 5.5, which is 5 hours 30 minutes.
maths.context: Indian Standard Time is set by the Sun on the line 82.5 degrees east. The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, which is 15 degrees each hour.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the degrees by 15 turns a position on the map into hours of time, and shows where the odd number 5 hours 30 minutes comes from.

maths.problem: On an orange, the equator thread is 24 centimetres long and the 60 degree thread is 12 centimetres long. What fraction of the equator is the 60 degree circle? If the equator is carried at 1,670 kilometres an hour, how fast is the 60 degree circle?
maths.answer: One half, so about 835 kilometres an hour.
maths.explain: 12 is half of 24. A spot on a path half as long, covered in the same time, goes half as fast. Half of 1,670 is 835.
maths.context: In the Orange Earth test, you measure circles at three latitudes. Every spot goes round once in 24 hours.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two lengths as a fraction shows how much slower one place goes than another, without needing a speedometer.

maths.problem: The equator is about 40,000 kilometres around. A person there goes round once in 24 hours. About how many kilometres an hour is that? Round your answer to the nearest 10.
maths.explain: Try 24 times 1,600. That is 38,400, which is a bit short of 40,000. Try 24 times 1,700. That is 40,800, which is a bit too much. So the answer is between 1,600 and 1,700, near 1,667. To the nearest 10, that is 1,670.
maths.context: Every place on Earth makes one turn a day. On the equator, that is a full circle of about 40,000 kilometres.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a time gives a speed, and rounding keeps the answer simple for a number we only know roughly.

maths.problem: India is about 29 degrees wide from east to west. The Earth turns 1 degree in 4 minutes. How long is the gap between the Sun's highest moment in the far east and in the far west? Give your answer in hours and minutes.
maths.explain: 29 times 4 is 116. 116 minutes is 60 plus 56, which is 1 hour 56 minutes.
maths.context: India stretches from about 68 degrees east to about 97 degrees east, and all of it uses one clock.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the width by 4 shows how much of a gap in Sun time hides behind one shared clock, and writing it in hours and minutes makes it easy to picture.

maths.problem: A day on Jupiter is about 10 hours. How many Jupiter days fit into one Earth day of 24 hours? Give the answer as a decimal.
maths.explain: 10 goes into 24 two times, with 4 left over. 4 out of 10 is 0.4. So the answer is 2.4.
maths.context: Jupiter spins once in about 10 hours, much faster than the Earth.
maths.why_maths: A decimal shows exactly how much faster a planet turns than the Earth, in a single number you can compare.

maths.problem: A child weighs 30 kilograms at the North Pole. Because of the Earth's spin and bulge, they weigh about 0.5 percent less at the equator. How many grams less is that?
maths.explain: 30 kilograms is 30,000 grams. 1 percent of 30,000 is 300. Half of 300 is 150.
maths.context: The spin flings things outward a little, and the Earth bulges at the equator, so gravity is a tiny bit weaker there.
maths.why_maths: Finding a small percentage shows how tiny the effect of the spin is, which is why we never feel it.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart of the circle lengths a child measured on an orange. How many times longer is the equator circle than the 60 degree circle?
maths.explain: The equator bar is 26 and the 60 degree bar is 13. 26 divided by 13 is 2. So the equator circle is twice as long.
maths.context: In the Orange Earth test, you measure circles at the equator, 30 degrees and 60 degrees north. The chart shows made-up results.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time most people pictured the Earth as a perfect ball. In 1672, French astronomer Jean Richer took a pendulum clock to Cayenne, near the equator. It lost about two and a half minutes a day compared with Paris, as if gravity were weaker there. In 1687, Isaac Newton explained why. A spinning ball of rock and water must bulge at its middle, as soft clay does. Yet the Cassini family in France measured the ground and believed the Earth was longer from pole to pole, like a lemon. In 1735 and 1736, the French Academy sent two expeditions to settle it. One went to Peru near the equator. The other went to Lapland, far in the north. Both measured the ground length of one degree of latitude. The degree in Lapland was longer, which means the ground curves less near the pole. The Earth is flatter at its poles, as Newton said. The French writer and scientist Émilie du Châtelet, who later translated Newton's book into French, had argued for his side.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Richer, Isaac Newton, and the French Academy expeditions led by Pierre Louis Maupertuis and Charles Marie de La Condamine
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many French scientists, including the Cassini family, believed the Earth was longer from pole to pole than across the equator, like a lemon. The two expeditions showed that it is flattened at the poles, and wider at the equator, because it spins.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Five Noons needs sunrise and sunset times, which come from a weather app, a newspaper weather box or a call to a relative in another city. The noon gaps should come out near 13, 46, 62 and 75 minutes after Guwahati for Kolkata, Chennai, Kochi and Mumbai, give or take two minutes because apps round times. The sunrise gaps will look untidy, because sunrise also depends on how far north a city is and on the season, and the steps say so. The Orange Earth uses a large orange. The 30 degree circle should be about 85 to 90 out of 100 of the equator and the 60 degree circle about half. On the small circles, mark dots and join them instead of using a rubber band, which slides. The Extra Turn needs a clear floor of about 3 metres. Star Gate depends on clear nights and a view of a fixed edge, so the steps say what to do when clouds stop you, and give the planetarium as a fallback. The Night Watch needs a grown-up, and the lamp challenge uses only a torch and paper. Facts to check before the unit goes live: that British India adopted one standard time in 1906; that Assam tea gardens keep garden time one hour ahead of Indian Standard Time; the 2011 Japan earthquake figure of about 2 millionths of a second; the 2016 figure of more than 80 percent of people under brightened skies; the Moon's drift of about 3.8 centimetres a year; the weight difference of about half a percent between pole and equator; that Emilie du Chatelet translated Newton's Principia into French; and the Richer pendulum figure of about two and a half minutes a day. The longitudes of the cities are rounded to one decimal place. The videos have no address yet.
